This study investigates the generalised multiple Arnold theorem in relation to 
optimisation problems, specifically for objective functions that depend on 
parameters. We establish a connection between the ground state of a certain 
mathematical operator and a particular space of functions that depend on 
those parameters, thereby extending previous work by Tezuka and Yamaguchi. 
Additionally, this outcome has a significant implication for the optimisation 
of certain types of functions, revealing the existence of a optimal solution that 
can be characterised by its relationship with a specific set of functions. 
Moreover, this finding can be further refined by categorising the functions 
according to their respective growth rates. Ultimately, this result can be viewed 
as a more general and extensive version of the original Arnold theorem. 
Furthermore, this study also explores the connection between the optimisation 
problems and the space of polynomials with varying degrees, revealing new and 
unexplored properties. Interestingly, this study reveals that the optimisation 
problems can be viewed from two distinct perspectives, namely, a generalised 
version of the classic Arnold theorem and a specialised version of the 
generalised Arnold theorem itself. 
Furthermore, this study also delves into the computational aspects of the 
optimisation problems in question and demonstrates that certain methods, 
including deep learning techniques, can be employed to tackle them. 
Interestingly, the results obtained through these methods reveal intriguing 
patterns and trends that are not explicitly stated in the main findings of 
the study. 
Lastly, this study also explores the connection between the optimisation 
problems and the space of polynomials with varying degrees by employing a 
uniquely novel approach, namely, a reverse mathematical exploration, in which 
the study seeks to establish the existence of the optimal solution by assuming 
its opposite, thereby mirroring the typical process in classical 
mathematical research. 
Ultimately, this study can be viewed as an endeavour to extend the realm of 
pure and applied mathematics, encompassing not just the generalised Arnold 
theorem but also its computational aspects and the space of polynomials with 
varying degrees, thereby expanding the frontiers of both theoretical and 
computational mathematics. 
Furthermore, this study also delves into the connection between the 
generalised Arnold theorem and the space of polynomials with varying degrees 
as a means to gain a deeper understanding of the latter, thereby shedding light 
on its inherent properties and characteristics. 
Lastly, this study can be viewed as a tribute to the foundational work of 
Vladimir Arnold

gap between the present state and the ultimate goal of comprehensive models.

A novel set of equations governs the statistical properties of the longest path to a leaf in a randomly generated permutation. The significant path's distribution asymptotically simplifies to a normal distribution, with which the equations' solution yields the exact mean and variance. The same framework also applies to the pairwise comparison tree used in the Medusa algorithm, a sorting method discovered by Darrell Hankerson, Mike Jacobs, and Stephen Kruska in 1989. The equations derived for this tree yield a gamma distribution in place of the normal distribution. The behavior of this distribution can be described as a mixture of two distinct patterns, depending on the size of the permutation: for smaller permutations, it closely resembles a normal distribution, whereas larger permutations exhibit a clear mixture of two distinct distributions. The exact values obtained from solving the equations perfectly match the asymptotic results of the random permutation or pairwise comparison tree model. The provided numerical results verify that the size of the longest path to a leaf, when normalized by the logarithm of the permutation size, follows a normal distribution for permutations and a gamma distribution for pairwise comparison trees. The derived equations are analogous to the Bethe approximation equation used in the context of mean-field theory and the deranged ladder model equation. The exact numerical results obtained from solving the equations match the asymptotic results of the random permutation or pairwise comparison tree model, with the latter's results possibly being the result of a limiting process towards the deranged ladder model. The exact numerical results are in line with the scaling exponent found in the study by S. N. Majumdar and G. R. Akutsu for the deranged ladder model. The findings also demonstrate that the mean and variance of the longest path to a leaf in the pairwise comparison tree model match the mean and variance of the pairwise comparison tree used in the Medusa algorithm developed by Darrell Hankerson, Mike Jacobs, and Stephen Kruska. A strong Gelfand pair (G,H) is defined by a group G and subgroup H, 
with every irreducible character of H resulting in a multiplicity-free 
character of G. Specifically, we identify the strong Gelfand pairs of SL(2, 
p) when p is a prime number. There are six such pairs, each with a 
subgroup index of 2. We also calculate and present the irreducible 
character tables for these subgroups. Furthermore, we outline an approach 
to computing all the character tables of their corresponding subgroups 
of indices 2, 3, and p. This method is initially applied to SL(2, 2) and SL(2, 5). 

We also establish the classification of transitive permutation groups of 
indices 2, 3, and p in SL(2, p), with a notable result that a transitive 
permutation group of index p in SL(2, p) is a split extension of ZSL(2, p) by a generalized Frobenius group of order p^2. 

In the process, we introduce a novel concept of a weak Bruhat order, which may be of independent interest. 

We further generalize the concept of strong Gelfand pairs to GL(n, p), but only partially, as we do not identify all such pairs. However, we compute the irreducible character tables for subgroups of indices 2 and 3 in GL(2, 2) and GL(2, 5). 

Lastly, we outline an open problem related to the classification of strong Gelfand pairs in GL(2, p).

We utilized the quark model to calculate electrostatic form factors for isoscalar pentaquark states with unique characteristics, specifically those containing $c c$ pairs and strange quarks. This research is crucial for understanding the composition and spatial arrangement of these exotic states and can contribute to identifying their signatures at future electron-ion colliders. By analyzing the response patterns of these states to electromagnetic interactions, we distinguished between diquark and meson-like behaviors, thus shedding light on the underlying pentaquark structure. Our findings also compared theoretical results with available experimental data. Furthermore, we suggest that differential cross section measurements in electron-kaon collisions could provide direct evidence for the existence of isoscalar pentaquark states. This could be achieved by detecting $D$ meson production in both planar and non-planar configurations. This study serves as a starting point for developing comprehensive theoretical frameworks to explore the electromagnetic properties of these enigmatic states. Future studies will delve into the photoproduction of pentaquark states and investigate their decay properties. This broader research aims to provide a more accurate understanding of these extraordinary states. Experimental verification of our predictions through precise measurements at future electron-ion colliders, such as the future Electron-Ion Collider (EIC), is highly anticipated. This includes the potential for the LHC to detect exotic particles that are currently inaccessible due to their short lifetimes. This study is part of a larger research initiative focusing on the Jefferson Lab's future Electron-Ion Collider (EIC) and the FCC-ee, a proposed high-luminosity electron-positron collider under consideration by CERN. This broader research aims to explore a range of complex topics, including charm-quark physics, baryon spectroscopy, and the properties of exotic states, with particular emphasis on the unique capabilities of the FCC-ee in the heavy-flavor sector. This paper proves that any finite-dimensional Zinbiel algebra over a given field possesses a specific characteristic - nilpotency, building on a previous discovery that these algebras are solvable. To further this research, a new algebraic structure, the Derived algebra, is introduced, leading to the identification of a first infinite set of equivalent properties, including but not limited to, P-differential, P-alternating, and nilpotent properties. Interestingly, this classification also reveals the non-uniqueness of quasiprime properties in the context of finite-dimensional algebras. Additionally, this research defines and explores the properties of infinite-dimensional Zinbiel algebras, identifying distinct classes of these algebras based on their characteristic properties. Specifically, it is discovered that a previously defined algebra, the algebra of skew polynomial mappings, is both finite-dimensional and nilpotent. Lastly, this research delves into the characteristics of commuting and nilpotent-derived algebras when their properties coincide. This research examines the scattering theory for a cubic, spatially varying Schrödinger equation with an inverse square potential: $iu_t + \Delta u - \frac{a}{|x|^2}u = \lambda |x|^{-b} |u|^2u$ with $a > -\frac14$ and $0 < b < 1$ in 3D space. The paper establishes global solvability and scattering in the energy space $H^1_a(\mathbb R^3)$ for all initial conditions in the defocusing scenario, whereas in the focusing scenario, it proves scattering for data below a threshold by leveraging a virial/Morawetz method. The proof relies on a new approach of modified Strichartz estimates in weighted Sobolev spaces. The outcome represents a generalization of the findings in J. Bourgain and N. Van den Berg's paper. The same approach can be applied to the case of the radial restriction of the defocusing cubic radial defocusing Gross-Pitaveskii model. The outcome extends previous work in L. Chen, N. Visciglia, and W. Zhan's paper and confirms the results in B. Dodson and D. I. Kim's paper for radial scenarios. The study also addresses the long-term behavior of the solutions and their rates of decay towards the ground state. The work ultimately leads to the construction of quasi-momentum maps for the given system, which in turn enables the application of variational methods to study the global solvability and scattering in the focusing scenario, particularly for solutions below a threshold, and to establish the link between the solutions' behavior and the properties of the ground state in the absence of defocusing effects. The outcome proves that the solutions' long-term behavior are determined by the interplay of defocusing and inverse square potential effects. The work extends previous work in L. Chen, N. Visciglia, and W. Zhan's paper and confirms the results in B. Dodson and D. I. Kim's paper for radial scenarios. The study ultimately generalizes the findings in J. Bourgain and N. The approach taken in this research can be applied to the case of the defocusing cubic radial defocusing Gross-Pitaveskii model.

The early K-type star K2-138, hosting six planets, particularly five that may be in a prolonged chain of 3:2 mean motion resonances, necessitates the analysis of its planets' potential resonant behavior. By utilizing existing data for each planet's mass and size, derived from light curve analyses and radial velocity measurements, our goal is to synthesize observations and analyze the system through a comprehensive modeling approach, incorporating the effects of tidal interactions and post-discourse star variability. Our analysis, encompassing over 1000 N-body simulations, suggests that approximately 85% of these simulations indicate a consecutive chain of 3:2 resonances among the planets of K2-138. However, detailed analysis reveals that this chain may be interrupted by "resonant skips" - instances where the planets bypass expected resonant configurations - and discrepancies in predicted planetary sizes when employing different analytical methods, prompting the need to consider the reliability of each approach's results. Furthermore, our findings indicate that the system may be experiencing signs of post-discourse star variability, potentially stemming from the disc-induced stellar spin-down. Ultimately, our study's findings highlight the importance of incorporating the effects of tidal interactions on the system, while also acknowledging existing uncertainties in the system's orbital parameters and the occurrence of resonant skips in the resulting simulations. As such, our analysis serves as a foundation for future investigations into the dynamics of K2-138, particularly in the context of potential additional resonances in this system. We establish connections between the Gelfand--Graev modules for central covers, the Euler--Poincar\'e polynomial of the Arnold--Brieskorn manifold, and the quantum affine Schur--Weyl duality via a permutation representation of the Weyl group, which governs these three objects. This permutation representation, called $M^\lambda$, is defined by a specific cohomology class in a simplified form of the Buchsbaum--Koszul complex associated with the Arnold--Brieskorn manifold. By analyzing the action of the Weyl group on $M^\lambda$ for each $\lambda$, we identify key submodules and determine the corresponding structures as free modules of the Weyl group. Building on these results, we derive explicit formulas for the Gelfand--Graev modules of one-dimensional central covers and show that their limits at infinite parameter match the corresponding components of $M^\lambda$ under specific generality conditions. Additionally, we extend our methods to compare local cohomology modules of the Spec of a finite type Z-algebra with its "deformed" Spec under a non-trivial change of monoidal structure. This comparison leads to a dual version of the quantum affine Schur--Weyl duality. Furthermore, by adapting our methods, we establish a local version of the quantum commutative Weil's conjecture. Ultimately, our results are used to compute the quantum Euler--Poincar\'e polynomial for specific one-dimensional central covers and recover B. Leung's results on the quantum Euler--Poincar\'e polynomial for one-dimensional cohomology covers. Furthermore, our results imply that his results hold more broadly under specific Weyl group generality conditions. The methods employed in this research combine both geometric and representation-theoretic techniques, including those from algebraic, Lie, and quantum group theories, as well as recent developments in representation of central covers. As supplementary materials, we provide detailed analysis of several key examples, including a comparison with recent results of D. Barcelo, D. N. Levine, and I. Strachan on the quantum Euler--Poincar\'e polynomial. Differentiating between Ih ice and hexagonal ice, previously identified as two distinct proton disordered phases, is essential. Employing the local order metric, which quantifies the likelihood of a proton participating in a tetrahedral configuration with three other protons, researchers found that tetrahedral configurations are rare in all studied phases. Notably, hexagonal ice exhibits a more tetrahedron-like structure than previously thought, while tetrahedral configurations in ice III, IV, and VI, as well as proton disordered fcc ice, are relatively common, occurring in approximately 50% of cases. These results challenge the current understanding of proton disordered phases, which may not always exhibit tetrahedron-like structures. Additionally, the study proposes a new phase boundary between tetrahedral and non-tetrahedral proton disordered states, which could have significant implications for the development of new experimental techniques to detect these phases. These results are particularly relevant for the study of tetrahedral configurations in high-pressure ice, as well as proton disordered phases at high temperatures, which may not produce distinct NMR signatures. The Isabelle Archive of Formal Proofs has amassed substantial size over recent years, with an ever-expanding collection of proven theorems and evidence. Despite the advantages this extensive library offers, such as clear documentation and rigorous verification, accessing specific parts becomes increasingly difficult due to its massive scale, making it harder to locate particular items or grasp the overall picture. To address these challenges, we propose the development of a search engine tailored to Isabelle's library, capable of efficiently identifying relevant content within the archive. In this paper, we detail the process of creating such an instrument by outlining a custom indexing tool that organizes the archive's content, including a functioning search engine. Our solution not only works in real-time but also contributes to a deeper comprehension and utilization of the archive's extensive knowledge. A newly established server is required to run the indexing tool in conjunction with a search engine, allowing users to access the archive despite the considerable time needed for the proof verification. In return, our approach not only enhances the search experience but also increases accessibility and comprehension of the archive's content. A comprehensive evaluation of our proposed solution, encompassing benchmarks, usability studies, and system administration insights, demonstrates its benefits, with results showing a notable improvement in search speed and efficiency. Our approach also showcases the archive's potential for further integration with external tools, such as Google Scholar, by integrating its API in the search engine framework. Ultimately, our approach not only enhances the search experience but also sheds light on the underlying complexities involved in creating a tailored search engine for the archive. As such, our approach contributes to a deeper comprehension and awareness of these intricate technical and social considerations. In situ data from the heliosphere is often used for observational analysis but produces complex time-series information that's more effectively interpreted as sound than visually analyzed. Audification is a straightforward way to turn oscillatory data into sound, but it's limitations enable further creative interpretation and analysis methodologies. This paper examines audio-based methods as tools for heliospheric science: audification's current utility, potential future applications, and using sound to facilitate scientific analysis and discussion. It also explores connections to broader fields like seismic exploration and medical imaging whereavers, sound waves, or other forms of oscillatory data are analyzed. Key topics covered include: 1) past and current uses of audification; 2) future developments and challenges; 3) employing advanced audio processing techniques to extract heliospheric science insights; 4) using sound to represent structure in data (rather than time-based activity) and related challenges; 5) the role of audio-based methods in scientific research; and 6) relevant resources and how to get involved. This document aims to stimulate discussion, gather input from the scientific community, and provide a reference for researchers entering the field. It's intended for researchers, scientists, and engineers across heliospheric science, geophysics, seismology, and other related fields, as well as broader audio-based communities. This document is a call for input and participation in the newly established HelioAudio working group, which is open to membership and contributions from the community. A new class of rotating black brane solutions, influencing both space and time, have been discovered. This includes solutions with charge, for up to four rotating dimensions. This kind of rotating charged black brane appears in various theories, like string theory's dilaton gravity theory. Differences arise based on the number of dimensions involved. For four dimensions, the minimum mass occurs when the charge and a single rotational speed are equal. This minimum mass decreases with increasing mass and charge. This research introduces a groundbreaking representation scheme for text based on cognitive memory, specifically designed for Korean language. By mimicking the storage and retrieval process in human memory, it redefines text understanding and generates novel models for text processing tasks. Our approach incorporates a structured framework with interconnected modules of semantic and syntactic information, mirroring the hierarchical organization of memory. To capture syntactic context, it employs a sequential representation scheme with an attention mechanism, utilizing limited contextual information for effective processing of long sequences. Additionally, it leverages parallel attention to efficiently retrieve relevant information from the extensive semantic module. Our evaluations on various tasks, including question answering, machine translation, and classification, demonstrate superior performance compared to existing Korean models, while the underlying framework can be easily extended to process other languages. In line with the project's goals, the implementation and source code are openly available on GitHub, aiming to support the development of more advanced Korean language processing systems. A small-step operational semantics in a programming language breaks down computations into discrete, indivisible steps, directly mirroring the language's operational instructions. Conversely, a big-step semantics views a computation as a completed, all-at-once process. Many programming languages, however, require the use of both semantics, as they cannot be adequately represented by just one. For example, languages with both nameless and named variable types present a problem when evaluating recursion, as nameless variables are evaluated before they can be used in a recursive call. To address this, a novel method is proposed that unifies small-step and big-step semantics into a single framework. This unification, achieved through the use of a relational semantics, allows for the representation of both discrete and complete computations simultaneously. The method is demonstrated with a Stalmarck-like semantics for a simple lambda calculus with nameless variables and recursion. The resulting static analysis can automatically eliminate redundant recursive calls from named recursive functions, as exemplified in Scheme. The method also offers an additional advantage in the form of a novel form of context-sensitive information, derived from the analysis of the relationships between the input and output states of a computation, which can further aid in the elimination of redundant recursive calls. The derived information is shown to satisfy a particular structure, namely being both function-level and context-sensitive, and it is hypothesized that this characteristic is unique to the method used. To validate the method, a number of tests were conducted, including both positive, which demonstrated its ability to accurately eliminate redundant recursive calls, and negative, which identified a number of limitations and edge-cases, such as the need to accommodate different evaluation strategies. The method was also compared with existing techniques, such as the application of the Stalmarck algorithm to the big-step semantics of a recursive nameless lambda calculus, and it was demonstrated that the novel method allows for the derivation of more precise information than would be possible with the application of the Stalmarck algorithm alone. The method was further validated by examining its ability to accommodate different evaluation strategies, such as the application of call-by-need evaluation methods, and it was demonstrated that the novel method allows for the derivation of more precise information than would be possible with the application of call-by-need alone. The method was also shown to be capable of handling a number of edge-cases, such as the application of call-time recursion, and it was demonstrated that the novel method allows for the derivation of more precise information than would be possible with the application of call-time recursion analysis alone. interactions between light and matter in motion.  One such phenomenon, the so-called
Fresnel-Fizeau effect, arises from the interaction between a moving dielectric medium and
light it carries, and results in a relative change in the light's phase.  A second, the
Bergeron effect, occurs when light travels through a medium in motion and, as a result,
experiences a change in its direction of propagation.  Both the Fresnel-Fizeau and
Bergeron effects are characterized as drag effects, and can be understood within the
framework of a generalized dielectric tensor that takes into account the motion of the
material.  While the effects are typically observed in systems with two levels of
freedom, research has demonstrated the possibility of observing both effects within
a single system.  A new study has demonstrated the Fresnel-Fizeau and Bergeron effects
in a system consisting of chiral Bose-Einstein condensates, where the drag effects are

drag effects, are described using a generalized dielectric tensor, and are found to be
in line with theoretical predictions.  A notable characteristic of the system is the
presence of drag effects in systems lacking optical activity and circular birefringence.

Existing exact algorithms for these problems are computationally resource-intensive, partly due to their increased complexity following reformulation of the problem, and partly due to unknown bounds for binary variables. In contrast, we suggest a Lagrangian dual approach that separates variable bounds without increasing the problem's size, reducing the computational burden compared to dual-based algorithms used for linear relaxation. This method turns an intractable optimization problem into a series of tractable ones, where each solution yields an upper bound unless a certificate of optimality is found, indicating the boundedness of the original problem. This method also offers a straightforward way to obtain a lower bound when it fails to do so. In addition, we outline potential extensions to address mixed-integer variables and provide numerical results demonstrating its efficiency. This method is particularly relevant for problems with uncertain binary variables, but can also be applied to those with uncertain continuous variables when bounds are present. Furthermore, it is shown that this method yields better results than assuming the worst-case scenario, both in terms of runtime and solution quality. This paper explores the potential of transfer learning in GNNs via adaptive GNNs, allowing the fine-tuning of pre-trained models on novel domains. This approach not only reduces the need for large labeled data but also makes it easier to understand the learning process. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of adaptive GNNs, particularly with pre-training using node and graph-level encoders. By applying adaptive GNNs to the SemEval-2019 Task 4, we achieve better performance using fewer labeled data compared to traditional supervised models. Moreover, our technique outperforms the existing state-of-the-art method, requiring fewer required instances. This new approach sheds light on transfer learning in the context of deep learning models operating in graph spaces. Code for the adaptive GNNs can be accessed at https://github.com/sochr/adaptive-gnn. Additionally, our project also includes a graph-based API for state-of-the-art GNN models used in this study, which can be found at https://github.com/sochr-graph-gdub. This API facilitates seamless model selection and configuration to address a variety of tasks, ultimately enhancing the learning process for graph-based deep learning models. Lastly, our work includes a curated dataset of anti-Semitic text, which may be of independent interest and utility due to its unique content and the difficulty in detecting hate speech, particularly in the Hebrew language, where there are limited resources available compared to other languages. This dataset can be accessed at https://github.com/sochr-graph-gdub. Ultimately, our research contributes to the development of the graph deep learning field by introducing the graph deep API and presenting a new approach to transfer learning in graph spaces. This new understanding not only empowers researchers to explore novel applications of graph neural networks but also inspires the creation of additional resources, such as the graph deep API and the curated anti-Semitic dataset. Lastly, our research sheds light on the potential of adaptive graph neural networks to address a range of tasks, including the identification of hate speech, a particularly challenging task due to its prevalence (frequency) and the scarcity of resources in the Hebrew language. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of adaptive graph neural networks, achieving results comparable to state-of-the-art models, often requiring fewer required instances. To do this, we use a Bayesian double feature allocation model that groups users and items according to their shared characteristics, where each group represents a distinct feature. By collecting data on user interactions, we update the Bayesian measurements to determine the probability of users and items being part of a particular feature. As predicting user preferences requires simultaneous user and item predictions, the incorporation of a data augmentation step is necessary to address the challenge of predicting items lacking user feedback. Additionally, the model's natural extension to multi-modal settings allows it to effectively combine information from different input sources. Furthermore, we present an efficient sampling-based inference technique that makes it feasible to implement and train the model on large-scale collaborative filtering datasets. Ultimately, our approach yields improved predictive accuracy and efficient inference for collaborative filtering tasks. One of the fundamental issues in the study of streaming algorithms is determining memory efficiency for discovering areas with dense occurrences in datasets. This problem is referred to as detecting heavy hitters and involves finding dataset elements that exceed a given frequency threshold. In a recent study, the authors presented a first set of O(1/ε) memory-efficient one-pass streaming algorithms for discovering the existence of heavy hitters with optimal space usage, and these algorithms were later expanded to account for $\\eta$-$\\ho$ heavy hitters, requiring a unique quantifier function. However, the existence detection algorithms for $\\eta$-$\\ho$ heavy hitters required either multi-pass or increased memory capacity, and the authors were only able to develop a one-pass streaming algorithm for univariate $\\eta$-$\\ho$, requiring a significant amount of memory, often O(1/ε^2) or more, to detect the possibility of heavy hitters across all possible quantifier functions. In contrast, this paper presents a set of one-pass streaming algorithms for discovering both univariate and multivariate $\\eta$-$\\ho$ heavy hitters with a more efficient memory usage, often O(1/ε) or less, and these algorithms are applicable to a broader range of quantifier functions. These new algorithms are derived from a novel problem, referred to as the Optimal Partitioning Problem (OPP), and a subsequent development of a streaming algorithm for solving the OPP over streams of integers in O(1/ε) memory usage, where ε represents the inverse of a given parameter representing the desired subspace occupancy. The momentum-dependent structure of the static magnetic susceptibility in Heisenberg magnets is investigated using the Bethe-Salpeter equation with a specific type of vertex that is constrained by the Ward-Takahashi relation. It's found that the susceptibility exhibits a dependence on momentum that varies as $q^2/\xi^2$ at large momentum levels, where $\xi$ is the correlation length. Furthermore, an upper limit is established for the magnitude of this dependence, relative to the form that would result from a mean-field solution of the model. This dependence arises from interactions between fluctuating magnetic moments, and its magnitude is related to the ratio of the model's interaction strength to the inverse correlation length. An approach based on renormalization group theory is also used to analyze the model and account for its effects on the susceptibility's momentum-dependent structure. By considering the limits of strong and weak interactions, as well as the effects of expanding the model in the number of spin components, we find that the model exhibits a universal type of behavior, distinct from the behavior that would result from a mean-field solution or from applying the renormalization group to a different type of model. Our results are compared to experimental measurements of the susceptibility in various types of magnets and ferromagnets. However, previous model transformations being too restrictive hindered their widespread adoption. This led to the emergence of co-designed diffracts, lightening the constraints of model transformations by considering external interventions. Nevertheless, even co-designed diffracts still restrict the use of domain-specific language and services. To overcome this limitation, this work aims to make the initial delta lenses framework more applicable to complex model transformations by incorporating machine learning and related advancements. The research defines a new notion of delta lenses that can leverage machine learning and introduces various ways to utilize learning within this framework. The notion is examined through a model transformation known as DSL2toMQL, which translates concrete, domain-specific logic into an abstract, query language. The study demonstrates four implementations of delta lenses that utilize machine learning: two based on supervised learning and two based on unsupervised learning. The first two use neural networks, while the last two use clustering. The efficacy of these implementations is evaluated through experiments and practical applications in the context of a concrete, distributed DSL and a more fluid, domain-specific language. The research demonstrates that the proposed framework effectively facilitates the translation of various domain-specific languages and enhances the incremental and precise nature of model transformations. The study concludes by discussing the remaining hurdles associated with incorporating machine learning into delta lenses and future areas of investigation. The proposed framework is expected to significantly contribute to the domain of model-to-model transformations by facilitating the precise and incremental processing of multiple domain-specific languages and enhancing the scalability and adaptability of model transformations. The research findings are expected to facilitate the development of efficient model transformation tools and techniques that can be seamlessly integrated into various development environments, such as IDEs. The study demonstrates the potential of the proposed framework in empowering end-users to easily perform complex model transformations without requiring extensive technical knowledge. The research also highlights the importance of addressing the challenges of ensuring data consistency during model transformations. Furthermore, the proposed algorithm is also adaptable for calculating non-equilibrium solutions, thereby enabling accelerated convergence rates compared to the traditional iteration method. Moreover, the algorithm's capability to generate solution estimates of varying quality, based on the degree of rarefaction, is an added benefit. The theoretical underpinnings of the proposed algorithm are validated through its application in three distinct numerical examples. Firstly, the algorithm's ability to generate equilibrium solutions with maximum entropy is demonstrated through its application in test problems. Secondly, the algorithm's efficacy in solution estimates of varying quality, along with their convergence rates, is demonstrated through its application in test problems where the solution estimates derived from the algorithm differ from the target values. Lastly, the algorithm's accuracy in solution estimates and its convergence performance is demonstrated through its application in test problems. The Horizon-10T collaboration reported an observation of Multiple-Modal Hawking Radiation (MMHR) in which radiation emitted from a single black hole exhibited multiple peak intensities at varying frequencies.  To explain this phenomenon, we utilize the gravitational wave packet approach to simulate Hawking radiation, assuming that both black holes in a binary system emit Hawking radiation after merging.  Our simulation indicates that the Hawking radiation peaks are separated by intervals of $2\Delta\omega \approx 2c^3G^2M^4\Delta t^{-5}$, where $\Delta t$ represents the duration of the merger, and that the locations of these peaks can be predicted based on the characteristics of the merger and the detector.  Notably, the gaps between these peaks can be substantial, with a separation of $\Delta\omega \approx 10^{-4}$ eV$^{-1}$ for instance such as GW150914, corresponding to a peak intensity variation of $\Delta I \approx 10^{-5}$.  Our analysis suggests that such variations are common in Hawking radiation detected by LIGO/Virgo, and that they may be more pronounced in future detections by third-generation detectors such as the Cosmic Explorer and the International Gravitational System.  As such, MMHR could serve as definitive evidence of a clustering origin, and offers an additional means of studying the complex astrophysical origins of gravitational waves.  Moreover, the presence of Hawking radiation peaks at varying frequencies can be utilized to extract information about the properties of the black hole, such as its spin, and its age, which in turn can provide insight into the relevant astrophysical processes. Finally, separate channel analyses yielded similar results, allowing a joint analysis to establish evidence at a 3.4 standard deviation confidence level. Although not statistically significant, these findings indicate a Higgs-boson preference for coupling with bottom quarks over muons in tau particles. This research focuses on few-shot learning, where models must classify tasks with limited data, typically defined within an intrinsic space by prototypes and class labels. Prototypes are central to few-shot learning, but their optimization is often manually configured or calculated solely based on the labeled dataset. Our approach identifies that incorporating both labeled and unlabeled data within the few-shot learning framework can enhance generalizability. We propose Proto+++, which formalizes this understanding by using both sets of data to create more accurate prototypes. Our method iteratively refines prototypes with labeled data, and utilizes both labeled and unlabeled data mean and prototype distances to predict the unlabeled data labels in an entropy-minimizing process. Our experiments on various few-shot learning datasets demonstrate that Proto+++ consistently surpasses existing state-of-the-art methods. Our findings also reveal that incorporating unlabeled data can unexpectedly improve few-shot learning performance even with suboptimal labeled data configurations. This peak efficiency was primarily attributed to lower-order mode interactions. Both problems involve selecting items from a catalog to place in a container of limited capacity, with the goal of maximizing a measure of value without exceeding the capacity and ensuring a minimum value of non-zero value is achieved. SUKP considers item values and weights, while BMCP considers value and coverage value. We examine two variants of each problem that involve decision-making: allowing or not allowing selecting a single item, and allowing or not allowing selecting a subset of items. We use reduction arguments to demonstrate the complexity of each problem variant and prove either NP-hardness or NP-hardness conditional on the existence of subexponential-time or quasi-PSPACE many-one reductions. To promote safe cycling, our study develops an image-based system that evaluates route safety by identifying high-risk sections. This system identifies hazardous spots along a route, taking into account the existing bike infrastructure. Trained on a dataset of annotated cycling paths, our model identifies critical components such as cyclists and horizontal guide lines in images, and maps them into a representative position. By comparing the distance between the cyclist and nearest safety feature, and whether the guide line is intact or broken, our model determines risk scores for individual sections. The final step involves combining these scores to identify high-risk routes and route segments. This system shows strong performance on test data, with a $+5.5\%$ average AP compared to existing methods, and in particular, significantly improves the classification of very low-risk routes, reaching a high AP of $89.4\%$ while maintaining a low FP rate at $10.3\%$. Additionally, our model's interpretability is demonstrated by the identification of near-miss incidents in the CamCycle dataset. Furthermore, our analysis reveals that the system's performance can be further enhanced by incorporating additional data sources, such as open street maps and social media, which can help address data imbalance issues and improve model generalizability. The proposed system achieves AP of $73.5\%$ on the CamCycle test set, and reaches AP of $83.5\%$ when supplemented with additional data. This work contributes to the field of cyber physical systems by providing a novel solution to safe cycling navigation. A novel method using the RRT algorithm is introduced to create a safety-critical path by enforcing Control Barrier Functions and robot kinodynamic constraints while minimizing computation. This path planning framework incorporates robust Control Barrier Functions to account for uncertainties, ensuring the generated path is free from obstacles and adaptable to model inaccuracies. By integrating this approach, paths that are both safe and optimal are prioritized over collision-free paths that are overly cautious due to conservative system models. Additionally, this approach accommodates complex robot dynamics, including state-dependent inputs and nonlinear dynamics. Numerical simulations and real-world experiments on a mobile robot demonstrate the efficacy of this approach, outperforming state-of-the-art methods by significant margins in both scenarios. This approach's efficacy is further validated by its successful application in a mobile robot navigation task. This method showcases a harmony between optimal motion planning and robust control techniques. This work appears in Proceedings of the 24th International Conference on Artificial Intelligence (AAAI 2017).

Recent research has shown that neural networks with optimizable parameters can produce robust predictions when subjected to adversarial noise. In this study, neural ODEs, a type of neural network, were found to naturally resist adversarial attacks due to their inherent properties. Specifically, the error between a sample modified by adversarial noise and its prediction by a neural ODE, remains bounded within a small range. This discovery led us to suspect that neural ODEs could fail to generalize properly on the test dataset due to overfitting to adversarial noise. By examining the behavior of neural ODEs in this context, we gained a deeper understanding of their potential weaknesses, and identified a critical threshold for the amplitude of adversarial noise above which the error becomes excessively large. Additionally, we found that neural ODEs tend to produce inaccurate predictions when confronted with sudden, rapid changes in the adversarial noise. By investigating these characteristics, we were able to devise novel adversarial techniques specifically designed for neural ODEs, and demonstrate their effectiveness on real-world datasets such as CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100. Ultimately, our research revealed that while neural ODEs may naturally resist certain types of adversarial attacks, they are by no means universally secure. On the contrary, we found that they are particularly vulnerable to sophisticated attacks, and that existing defenses against adversarial noise in neural networks are ineffective in this context. We investigate the straight-line dynamics on a particular type of surface known as dilation surfaces. These surfaces are defined by taking a compact surface and embedding it in a higher-dimensional space, then tracing lines as they move away from a given point on the surface. Unlike translation surfaces, where straight lines change direction via discrete jumps, on dilation surfaces, changes in direction occur incrementally over an infinite series of smaller and smaller steps. Focusing on the dynamics driven by this process, we examine the set of all possible directions in which lines can move, along with the associated abelian actions inherent in this system. Our main finding is the presence of nontrivial, invariant directions in which lines do not change, as well as a wide range of directions in which lines move according to a linear pattern, with the rate of change determined by the surface's defining structure. We also demonstrate that the set of directions in which lines do change is inherently countably infinite, with each direction corresponding to a particular point on the surface, along with a unique trajectory associated with that direction. Furthermore, we show that the linear nature of the dynamics in certain directions allows for the existence of particularly structured forms of motion, known as translations and rotations. In certain cases, the set of directions in which lines do not change, along with the associated translations and rotations, satisfies a particular condition, leading to the system's integrability. Notably, dilation surfaces provide a new and significant class of examples, distinct from the previously known examples of tori and standard flat surfaces. In particular, the system of directions on which lines do not change, along with the associated translations and rotations, can be shown to be uniquely defined by the surface's structure, with the associated trajectories, known as leaves, being uniquely defined up to a certain degree of equivalence. Notably, the system of directions on which lines do not change is inherently sensitive to the choice of point around which the lines move, with the associated translations and rotations being uniquely defined only when a particular condition is met. In general, the system of directions on which lines do not change fails to exhibit the necessary degree of coherence, with the associated translations and rotations failing to satisfy certain necessary conditions, such as the linear gap condition, that would lead to the system's integrability. Recent studies have highlighted the limitations of traditional functional connectivity measures like correlation and information flow in brain networks.  Conventional approaches often generate contradictory findings when structural integrity is compromised, yet individuals with damaged brain structures still exhibit preserved cognitive functions.  This suggests the need for a more sensitive functional connectivity measure.  Inspired by Granger causality, total correlation theory offers potential as a more effective framework for assessing functional networks.  In this study, we investigate the potential of total correlation as a functional connectivity measure in brain networks, supported by an anatomical framework.  We simulate damage to distinct brain regions using Granger, and show that this simulation allows for a more nuanced distinction between non-functional and functional connections, ultimately contributing to a deeper understanding of functional connectivity assessment.  This research provides valuable insights for developing novel methods for measuring functional networks.  Furthermore, we hope that our work will encourage the integration of total correlation into various neuroimaging studies.  Ultimately, our study contributes to the ongoing discussion regarding the optimization of functional connectivity measurement methods in brain networks. Predictive distributions in Gaussian processes are impossible to calculate exactly, necessitating the use of Monte Carlo methods like random finite elements, Laplace approximation, and slice sampling, which have their own limitations. Monte Carlo methods provide a practical approximation but can be slow for larger inputs. This paper introduces the Gaussian process variational quantum algorithm, a quantum-inspired approach that utilizes variational quantum algorithms to simulate Gaussian process posterior distributions. This algorithm is compatible with both near-term quantum and classical computers, offering a potential alternative to traditional Monte Carlo methods. Experimental results on regression problems indicate that the quantum-inspired method surpasses classical Monte Carlo methods while suggesting that a genuine quantum algorithm might also outperform it. To accelerate policy optimization in complex, dynamic environments with limited sample sizes, reinforcement learning algorithms frequently employ experience replay.  These algorithms collect and reuse past episodes to compensate for limited sample availability.  However, the effectiveness of standard experience replay is constrained by its use of a fixed, uniform sampling method.  This leads to a lack of adaptability, as the same importance is given to all experiences without regard for their actual value.  Our proposed approach, adaptive experience replay, dynamically selects experiences based on their current relevance, leveraging their full potential to enhance sample efficiency and achieve optimal results.  Our research, though primarily focused on continuous control tasks in environments with varying levels of difficulty, indicates that adaptive experience replay is a universally beneficial approach, one that can be seamlessly integrated into existing methods with minimal modification to improve overall performance.  Our results demonstrate that adaptive experience replay surpasses the performance of standard experience replay, often by a substantial margin, across a range of environments and baseline reinforcement learning algorithms.  Our research further reveals that adaptive experience replay is a flexible approach that can be applied to a range of reinforcement learning tasks, including those characterized by changing conditions, multiple agents, and tasks with multiple objectives.  Our findings suggest that the effectiveness of adaptive experience replay is largely determined by its ability to prioritize experiences with the highest expected future returns.  As such, the adaptive experience replay approach presents a universal and efficient technique for enhancing reinforcement learning performance that can be easily integrated into a wide range of existing algorithms. Two new approaches have been developed to apply the supersymmetry method from Gaussian matrices to broader rotation-invariant real symmetric matrices. Specifically, we present a generalized approach that incorporates the supersymmetry method into Wigner semi-circle matrices via a novel transformation, and a conventional approach that utilizes the supersymmetry method directly in rotation-invariant real symmetric matrices. We demonstrate the effectiveness of these methods by calculating supersymmetric partition functions for specific scenarios, and validate the results by comparing them with analytical or numerical calculations based on determinantal point process methods. Furthermore, our approach allows us to establish a link between the supersymmetric method and the Oganesyan-Vanderbilt criterion, thereby providing an alternative perspective on the interplay between localization and delocalization phenomena. Specifically, we show that the supersymmetric method's critical point corresponds to the point where the participation number transitions from being finite to approaching zero as localization deepens. By analyzing the supermatrices, which are at the heart of the supersymmetric method, we gain a deeper understanding of their structural properties, thereby shedding light on their eigenvalue density, which is revealed to be a modification of the Wigner semi-circle distribution. Notably, the maximum of the resulting eigenvalue density occurs at a point that can be interpreted as a form of mean-level repulsion, even in the presence of localization. By exploring the eigenfunction properties, we find that the fluctuations of the eigenfunctions around zero are capped by a factor that is proportional to the square root of the system size, which is indicative of a form of spatial mean-field behavior. Moreover, the eigenfunctions' behavior near the Fermi level is characterized by a slow decay, which is within a power proportional to the distance from the Fermi level and inversely proportional to the system size. By analyzing the eigenfunctions' fluctuations, we discover that the eigenfunctions' slow decay is accompanied by a form of spatial anti-correlation, which is within a power proportional to the system size, which is indicative of a form of spatial quasi-monodromy. By calculating the fluctuations of the eigenfunctions' amplitude, we establish that the eigenfunctions' amplitude is bounded by a modified Bessel function, which is characteristic of a form of spatial quasi-monodromy. This paper addresses the challenge of forecasting spatiotemporal sequences using a novel approach called spatiotemporal predictive learning (ST-PL). Proposed goals in this framework include accurately predicting sequence-based queries such as location-based data like air quality or traffic speed. Existing machine learning methods face limitations in this domain due to their focus on classification tasks, which hinders their performance in forecasting tasks. In contrast, stochastic differential equations (SDEs) offer a promising solution by modeling dynamic behavior over time and space. This paper contributes several key advancements: integrating spatial features into stochastic differential equations; reducing the computational burden in forecasting by employing a numerical method; and merging spatial and temporal features in forecasting. Experimental results validate the proposed approach's effectiveness in forecasting spatiotemporal sequences. The associated code and data are publicly accessible at \url{https://github.com/Research-ST-PL}. Additionally, this research received funding from the European Union's Horizon2020 program under grant agreement 825240. Lastly, this paper's contributions are further enhanced through visualizations and videos available at \url{https://research-st-pl.github.io}.

This research focuses on bridging the gap between programming languages employing garbage collection for memory management and those leveraging advanced type systems to ensure memory safety in imperative languages. Historically, garbage collection has been used in functional languages, while imperative languages increasingly utilize type systems to safeguard memory usage. Our investigation applies existing methods for guaranteeing memory safety in imperative languages to languages with garbage collection. This is achieved by introducing new constructs that permit explicit memory management and ensuring the program remains safe by eliminating memory leaks and data leaks. This approach is flexible, allowing the user to balance the level of memory safety assurance against potential performance losses. Specific outcomes of this research include the development of new extensions for the imperative languages C99 and Java, as well as the effective use of these extensions to guarantee memory safety in programs featuring common features with languages like JavaScript, Python, and C++. The resulting systems are known as MiC98, MiJava, and we evaluate their performance through a range of benchmarks. The performance evaluation demonstrates that the new constructs do not compromise program efficiency, with explicit memory deallocation typically occurring at the native garbage-collected level. This work paves the way for the memory-safe development of critical system applications using commonly used languages, thus ensuring memory safety without switching to a different programming paradigm. This study focuses on the analysis and enhancement of BERT models, specifically those applied to tasks such as question answering and document classification. Initially, we examine how BERT's pre-training objectives contribute to its overall performance and discover that second-order pre-training objectives like those of XLNet greatly improve BERT's language model capabilities. Furthermore, we propose a family of tasks known as Multi-BERT, which is well-suited for document classification, leading to the development of an enhanced classification model called MBERT-CNN. This MBERT-CERT model exhibits superior performance on datasets such as the Squad dataset and the NiuTE dataset. Meanwhile, the MBERT-CNN model demonstrates competitive results across a range of classification datasets. Finally, we investigate the effectiveness of integrating multiple BERT models, finding that a certain level of task-specific fine-tuning is necessary to achieve optimal performance. This task-specific fine-tuning is particularly pronounced in tasks like question answering, whereas a broader range of parameters is required for document classification. Overall, our research contributes to the advancement of BERT models through the exploration of pre-training objectives, task-specific fine-tuning, and the development of multiple BERT-based classification systems. The non-dispersive shallow water equations, widely used for tsunami prediction, have significant limitations when it comes to short wavelength phenomena below the threshold of dispersion. Below this threshold, dispersive models like the verified Madapusi-Nussenzveig and Beyerle-Gottlieb-Pfister equations accurately describe tsunami propagation. However, these models rely on negative frequencies and intrinsically define wave solutions using both positive and negative frequencies. In contrast, non-dispersive models, such as the Madapusi-Nussenzveig equation used by the Joint Institute for Marine and Atmospheric Research, can only accurately predict solutions up to a certain time point, after which they deviate due to neglecting negative frequencies. In practical applications, this results in lost energy and altered wave profiles. By applying the entropy maximum principle, we derive the density profile that defines jammed macrostates, which in turn allows us to determine the entropy associated with these configurations as a function of channel width. Our findings demonstrate that the disparity in disk sizes affects the location of the jamming transition, shifting it towards narrower channels, and significantly influences the volume of jammed configurations and their entropy. Notably, jammed entropies are found to be non-zero even at the width corresponding to the jamming transition, indicating a first-order phase transition between jammed and fluid states. To characterize this transition, we establish a pressure profile that is contingent upon channel width and disk size disparity. By analyzing the disk size disparity at the pressure peak, we identify a set of width values for which pressure profiles exhibit minima, accompanying changes in disk orientation. These features emerge from the competition between pressure exerted by the outer disks and the repulsive force between the inner disks, driven by the disparity in disk sizes. When the channel is sufficiently narrow, this disparity triggers a change in the disk of largest size passing through the channel, as well as the formation of pairs of disks in close proximity, both of which influence the pressure profile. By considering the force balance at the disk level, we derive equations governing the position of the pressure peak and the minimum pressure value, which are in agreement with numerical simulations for various channel widths and disk size disparities. Notably, when the channel width is sufficiently large, pressure profiles converge toward a size-disparity-dependent limit, characteristic of disks of identical sizes. This research explores a discrete-time demographic model that incorporates the psychological impact on adult interactions with their environment and the temporal effects of larval interactions. The psychological stress caused by environmental toxins is transferred to offspring, influencing their fitness and corresponding toxicity levels. The model accounts for time-dependent larval interactions through a coalescing transformation and incorporates nonlinear effects from adult interactions. Under certain conditions, the population's mean toxicity level converges to a unique equilibrium, and the distribution of toxicity levels follows a geometric series. Additionally, the probability of a large number of individuals experiencing similar toxicity levels approaches a Poisson distribution. Furthermore, the model includes a stochastic element, which accounts for the uncertainty in the population's toxicity measurement. Using numerical simulations, the model's parameters are estimated, and the model is validated using simulated data and real-world pollution data from the Hudson River, New York. The study found that the model effectively estimates the population's toxicity level but experiences challenges in estimating other demographic model parameters. This is attributed to the model's high sensitivity to the initial conditions of the system, which complicates the interpretation of early-time results and makes it difficult to accurately model populations with long histories of contamination. Nonetheless, the model was able to replicate the Hudson River's pollution trend, which has shown signs of stabilization since the 1990s as a result of conservation efforts. The study's findings highlight the importance of considering the psychological impact on demographic models to better understand and address environmental and ecological challenges. Hierarchical taxonomies have immense value in various applications, but their applicability is restricted by the costly and time-consuming process of manual maintenance. Current automated methods for taxonomy construction are limited in their representation capabilities, typically using a straightforward 'is-a' relationship in Euclidean space. This leads to difficulties in handling complex relationships and noisy data. We propose an innovative approach that leverages hyperbolic embedding to efficiently model hierarchical relationships, free from assumptions about the data's structure. This approach enables accurate prediction of unseen subsumptions, cross-domain relationships, and can adapt to new data. Comprehensive evaluations on diverse datasets confirm the superiority of our method over state-of-the-art solutions in taxonomy learning and related applications. Additionally, we release HOP, an open-source platform for hyperbolic ontology processing, to facilitate future research and enable more expressive ontology representation and reasoning. Radio sources powered by an Active Galactic Nucleus have significant magnetic fields influencing their polarization properties, affecting observations of sources smaller than one inch. By analyzing submillimeter frequencies, we can bypass the polarization effects of star-forming processes and gain insight into the AGN magnetic fields. Our submillimeter observations of 42 radio galaxies with deprojected polarization angles yielded 15 sources, and measurements were taken for 11 of them. By cross-referencing our sample with the submillimeter properties of local Seyfert galaxies, we found no correlation between the polarization angle and angular size, though large sources showed variable polarization properties. For sources smaller than 5 inches, the median polarization fraction was below 2%, indicating polarization is typically frequency-dependent. Our results align with theories suggesting AGN magnetic fields originate from black hole driven turbulence or magnetic flux preservation during the jet collapse. Future studies should leverage interferometric polarization capabilities to improve our understanding. Furthermore, the implementation of polarization analysis tools in mm-wave and submillimeter telescopes will be beneficial for future observations. Hidden Markov Models (HMMs) are a type of mathematical model that consists of an observed output variable influenced by an unobservable state variable. Typically, the observed output is a real-valued vector, whereas the state variable, also referred to as the label, is an unobservable categorical value. The traditional inference methods for HMMs often struggle when the number of possible state variables increases, as their efficiency declines rapidly as the number of categories increases. In this paper, a new approach to learning the parameters of an HMM, referred to as the relaxed HMM (RHMMS), is presented, that avoids this issue. RHMMS uses a lower and more efficient dimensionality approach to determine the number of HMM states, thereby facilitating the estimation of their parameters. By treating the number of HMM states as a random variable, using a categorical distribution, and applying a Laplace prior, the parameters of the HMM can be learned in an efficient manner. The approach also allows for the incorporation of an indicator variable to determine which observations are influenced by each state. As a result, the RHM method is well-suited for handling problems with a large number of categories, such as multi-label classification tasks, that often involve many possible categories. The approach is demonstrated to be effective on a variety of tasks including multi-label classification, image segmentation, and speech recognition. This representation accurately captures turbulence's essence, characterized by the shift from one coherent structure to another and rapid internal dynamics. Our analysis yields exact expressions for the turbulent transport operator without employing simplifying assumptions. In the limit where spatial and temporal locality prevail, our operator reduces to the conventional estimate of turbulent transport as a diffusivity tensor, with its components being the integrated velocity field auto-correlation. However, we highlight the substantial underestimation of turbulent transport capabilities if this operator is to be calculated solely based on that estimate. Examples are given to illustrate the significant impact of delayed non-local effects in specific directions and the importance of the initial history of velocity data, particularly when the size of the structures involved exceeds the size of the cells in the mesh. These examples emphasize the need to invest computational resources in solving the advection problem efficiently. In particular, we show that using an iterative red-black algorithm to advance the solution in time results in an error of about 13% after one time step, with the required number of time steps to achieve a 1% error being 64. Furthermore, we demonstrate that employing only the most recent velocity history (retaining data up to time $t-1$) results in an error of about 25%) when compared to retaining data up to time $t-10$ (with an error of 0.35%). In addition, we show that employing advanced time integration schemes like the Runge-Kutta method does not yield improved results compared to the first-order Euler method used in conjunction with the retained velocity history. In contrast, our exact expression for the turbulent transport operator shows that delayed non-local effects are substantial for all the examples examined. These results imply that efficient methods of solving the advection problem with the ability to accommodate arbitrary memory lengths and directions are required to accurately describe turbulent transport properties. Evaluating nuclear elastic scattering with a realistic approach to nucleon-nucleus scattering is challenging due to the difficulty in accurately modeling the nuclear wave function. Many phenomenological models rely on simplifications such as the peak approximation, which is often used in conjunction with the de Vi\`segr\'e method to determine optical potential parameters. However, this approach has limitations, particularly when applied to heavier targets, as it can result in significant discrepancies between calculated and observed cross sections. In an effort to enhance the accuracy of optical model calculations, an alternative method referred to as the integral equation method is explored. This approach involves directly integrating over the one-body density matrix element to determine the forward optical potential, eliminating the need for the peak approximation and associated simplifications. Furthermore, by utilizing the forward and reverse de Vi\`segr\'e transformations, the connection between the forward optical potential, one-body density, and forward going free wave is rigorously formulated. As such, the forward optical potential derived through this new approach is expected to be more directly tied to the nuclear wave function and, consequently, the one-body density. In this work, the forward optical potential derived via the integral equation method is compared with that obtained using the peak approximation for multiple isotopes of various masses, with the results indicating a notable improvement in performance for heavier targets when the integral equation method is employed. Subsequent calculations also demonstrate the potential to further refine the forward optical potential by accounting for target shell structure. Finally, the utility of the forward optical potential derived via the integral equation method as a phenomenological input for coupled-channels calculations is explored using the example of $\bethetha$-decay coupling effects on nuclear elastic scattering, with the results indicating a notable sensitivity to the target's shell structure in this context. In particular, the coupled-chodes calculation yields cross sections that are generally in better agreement with experiment than those obtained from single-energy optical model calculations. However, the magnitude of the OMP-derived coupled-chodes prediction is highly dependent on the target mass and can only improve the agreement with data by a factor of two or better for heavy targets with masses exceeding $A\approx 40$. In contrast, the effect of $\bethetha$-decay coupling on nuclear elastic scattering appears to be relatively minor in the case of $\gamma$-decaying $^7$Li. Ultimately, the approach discussed in this work is envisioned as a means of enhancing the accuracy of optical model calculations and, by extension, the coupled-channels method. Our proposed R\'enyi divergence based metric makes it possible to minimize the risk of identity revelation by modifying a location-based service's masking process. In comparison to prior approaches, our method does not rely on predefined groups of users or any assumptions about the underlying data distribution. Instead, our metric identifies an optimal masking technique through a conditional optimization problem that minimizes the divergence in masking quality while considering the uncertainty of the underlying data distribution. We apply the Viterbi algorithm to an exponential family representation of the R\'enyi divergence, resulting in an efficient and robust method for maintaining user anonymity. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach effectively protects users from spatio-temporal tracing attacks while maintaining high service quality. Furthermore, our method's uncertainty estimates enable informed trade-offs between service quality and user anonymity. In contrast to existing methods, our approach provides quantitative trade-off analysis rather than a simple on-off switch. Research suggests that resting-state functional MRI can identify differences in brain function between individuals with different conditions, such as schizophrenia and controls. To enhance statistical power, studies often combine data from multiple sites, which, however, introduces additional complexities including site-specific variations in data quality and differing demographic characteristics. In this research, we investigated the effects of multi-site data collection on resting-state functional connectivity on two levels: (1) by assessing the statistical power to detect differences in group-based functional connectivity metrics when data from multiple sites are used for single-site and multi-site studies; (2) by examining the consistency of functional connectivity metrics across sites to understand variability in multi-site studies. Our results show that increased statistical power from multi-site studies is limited due to the added within-site variability, but we also found that multi-site studies can provide valuable insights into the consistency of functional connectivity metrics across sites. Specifically, we identified regions of interest that showed consistent differences across sites and those that did not. Notably, the consistent regions included areas primarily associated with visual processing, such as the occipital lobe, while the regions that lacked consistency included areas related to executive functions, such as the anterior prefrontal cortex. These findings highlight the importance of considering site-specific variations in data collection and analysis procedures. Furthermore, we suggest that the regions showing inconsistent differences across sites may be more susceptible to external influences and less resilient to brain disorders or diseases. In conclusion, our research provides new insights into the characteristics of multi-site studies in resting-state functional connectivity research. Our findings can inform researchers and analysts on how to effectively utilize multi-site data to gain more accurate insights into brain function. Additionally, our research can help identify brain regions that are more adaptable and resilient to brain disorders or diseases. Our key contribution is the development of efficient, randomized algorithms that achieve optimal O(n log n) running time and O(log log n) efficiency in energy consumption and processing, respectively. These results surpass the current best outcomes over various communication networks and significantly improve the existing random walk-based counting algorithm's running time and energy usage. Function computation involves distributed algorithms that solve functions parameterized by global inputs, and we design a randomized solution for this problem with optimal outcomes. A proposed navigation framework addresses this gap by utilizing a pre-computed map and learning to adapt to changing obstacles along the way. In the context of multiuser MIMO, the task of jointly selecting users and precoding involves solving a massive underdetermined system of equations to reconstruct transmit vectors for active users. This can be reformulated as a combinatorial problem of selecting variables from a sparse system, which can be addressed through group sparsity-based approaches. Drawing inspiration from compressed sensing, we develop a framework for solving the joint user selection and precoding problem in MIMO systems. This framework relies on solving convex optimization problems that leverage group sparsity, which can be further constrained using per-user and per-base station conditions. This results in novel algorithms, which we refer to as GSP-BS and GSP-BS2, respectively. Our simulations demonstrate the efficacy of these algorithms in achieving superior performance gains under specific settings. Ultimately, our findings indicate that GSP-BS outperforms GSP-BS2 but incurs increased computational complexity. This research offers a first look at applying group sparsity-based techniques to the joint user selection and precoding problem in MIMO systems. As such, several aspects of these methods can be further optimized. Future work aims to address these limitations, which involve incorporating per-user channel estimates, per-base station power constraints, and optimizing precoder phase, which we refer to as the GSP-BS3 problem. This will involve leveraging machine learning and convex optimization techniques to address the resulting non-convex problem. Additionally, our findings will be used to inform the design of a new algorithmic framework for addressing the joint user selection and precoding problem in MIMO systems. This will provide a valuable contribution to the community, which will ultimately translate to performance enhancements for multiuser MIMO systems. Furthermore, our proposed framework has the potential for extension to other communication technologies, such as massive MIMO, full-duplex MIMO, and channel estimation, which presents a promising area for further exploration. This discovery led us to speculate that a specific twisted product operation could yield invariants for higher-order Vassiliev knots, which we have confirmed up to order six. The discovery of a twisted product invariant for 2-cocycles in knot space prompted an exploration of its charactristic properties, and we found it satisfies two key properties: closure invariance and the ability to combine with other such invariants through a twisted product.
