Crowdsourced image datasets, commonly utilized in practice, are often marred by inconsistencies, largely due to the lack of detailed image descriptions. Before these datasets can be employed effectively, they necessitate classification to determine the degree of noise present. Addressing this task is complicated by two key challenges: (1) the need to process datasets comprising numerous images, typically comprising hundreds of thousands of examples; and (2) accurately accounting for dataset noise while filtering out uninformative examples, as irrelevant features can mislead classification. To address these challenges, we introduce a novel, multi-level classification method, known as DeepClean. This approach leverages a two-stage process, commencing with the development of a deep metric learning algorithm for image pre-screening. Image subsets exhibiting similar noise levels are then identified through a deep clustering method, while a multi-level CNN architecture determines the optimal number of classes for each subset, thereby achieving deep clean images. Experimental results, encompassing both synthetic and real-world datasets, demonstrate the efficacy of our approach, as evidenced by superior performance and resource efficiency compared to the state-of-the-art method Deep Clustering Based Noise Reduction (DCBNR). Specifically, on the ImageNet dataset, we enhance the accuracy of a pre-trained VGG-16 model by approximately 3% and achieve a significant 77% reduction in training time compared to DCBNR. Similarly, on the Yahoo dataset, we enhance the state-of-the-art accuracy by approximately 10% and achieve a substantial 85% reduction in training time. These findings validate the effectiveness of our proposed approach. The code and dataset are publicly available at https://github.com/asharakeh/DeepClean. We investigate a novel category of nonlocal games that can be solved by detecting noisy maximally entangled states, representing two parties' qubits that have undergone random decoherence. These games encompass a broad range of problems, including a previously defined game associated with additive quantum codes and recently discovered quantum LDPC codes. The threshold for approximately solving these games is defined by a certain distance to the space of maximally entangled states under random Pauli rotations. To analyze this threshold, we develop a modified version of the density of states formula from random matrix theory, demonstrating that this formula remains asymptotically equivalent even when the distribution of states is dynamically changing over time. This finding has far-reaching implications, enabling us to establish that approximately solving the defined nonlocal games is unique to quantum computing and to characterize the approximate complexity of these games using a theoretical measure of quantum computing's computational power. Furthermore, our approach allows us to establish a lower bound on the approximate complexity of classical computation relative to the quantum version. Our results also provide an analytical explanation for a phenomenon observed in quantum LDPC codes, namely, the phenomenon of quantum LDPC codes' threshold approaching one, as well as offering a new theoretical framework for comparing the performance of classical and quantum systems. Large data-driven companies continue to face a problem in effectively improving A/B testing, specifically in identifying meaningful treatment effects with confidence. Current best practices in industry circles often prioritize simplicity and ease of implementation over statistical rigor in order to avoid frustrating false positives or costly resource requirements. This paper explores the limitations of the standard 95% confidence interval approach in A/B testing, which fails to provide optimal results even with standard sample sizes from popular software tools. To address this issue, we introduce a new method that leverages a combination of the Shapley fractionated allocation and generalized confidence intervals. This approach, which we call SHAPTE, offers superior performance and more accurate estimates of treatment effects, treatment effect probabilities, and prediction intervals. Furthermore, our results demonstrate that SHAPTE outperforms alternative confidence interval methods, including those proposed by Dukes et al. and Gajane and Heller, across a range of scenarios. To facilitate wider adoption, we provide a publicly accessible Python library, TeAsto, which includes the SHAPTE algorithm and supports a range of allocation methods, confidence intervals, and more advanced use cases. Additionally, the consequences of ending inflation at different times for the inflaton field are explored, particularly how the field's behavior after inflation can be influenced by various factors such as the potential for an open universe or remnants of the inflaton particle. This introduction serves as a primer for understanding more advanced topics in the field, including cyclic inflation, gravitational wave detection, the interplay between inflation and dark matter, and the anthropic principle. In contrast, semi-supervised mutual enhancement presents an alternative approach, leveraging source-domain labels and target unsupervised data in an iterative refinement process. This paper introduces Entropy-Driven Semi-Supervised Mutual Enhancement (EDSIME), a novel algorithm that enhances domain adaptation through cross-entropy maximization and feature extraction. EDSIME iteratively improves domain alignment and feature extraction using cross-entropy maximization and entropy minimization objectives, ultimately achieving better performance. Notably, EDIME outperforms existing self-supervised domain adaptation methods, demonstrating superior results on both semantic segmentation and image classification tasks across various domain adaptation settings. We have developed an abstract framework for assessing resources in multi-task scenarios. Our framework builds upon a quantum information metric, measuring relative entropy differences between invariant subsets of a theoretical model. This metric effectively handles complex resource combinations, even when individual components are impossible to isolate, and it's versatile enough to work with various theories beyond quantum information, such as classical or hybrid models. By utilizing our metric in combination with a family of useful transformations, we've shown that it accurately assesses the effects of these changes on resource combinations. In addition, we've demonstrated its practicality in evaluating geometric relationships between diverse theoretical models, such as classical, quantum, and continuous-variable systems. Our framework's utility is further exemplified by its ability to derive resource conditions for efficient distributed data manipulation, a fundamental problem in quantum communication. Ultimately, these findings highlight the potential of our metric to unify diverse theoretical models and facilitate resource analysis in complex information processing tasks. This research examines the impact of disorder on the corner states of two-dimensional higher-order topological insulators.  The study distinguishes between different types of disorder - one that affects hopping terms uniformly and another that randomly varies these terms - and investigates how these variations affect bulk and edge states.  The results show that disorder that uniformly affects hopping terms does not harm topological stability, as the Hamiltonian remains symmetric under charge conservation.  The corner states are protected by the bulk gap, and as long as the disorder does not close the bulk gap, it does not extinguish the corner states.  On the other hand, disorder that randomly varies hopping terms can collapse the bulk gap, but it cannot wipe out the corner states as long as there are multiple connection paths between corners.  The findings also highlight the significance of higher-order topological characteristics in ensuring the durability of corner states against disorder.  The study further explores the dynamic behavior of corner states in systems subjected to random variations of the on-site potential.  The results may have significant implications for experimental efforts to stabilize the corner states.  The study also delves into the analogy between the proposed insulating system and classical fixed-point networks, and discusses the potential for topological effects in the classical dynamics of these networks.  The research concludes by outlining potential experimental realizations of two-dimensional higher-order topological insulators. Time series analysis has become a crucial aspect of various scientific disciplines as it aims to uncover hidden patterns within sequences of data over time or chronological order. To address this need, a new statistical technique called Supervised Topographic Mapping Through Time (SGTM-TT) has been developed as a multivariate approach to time series analysis. By incorporating the principles of multidimensional scaling and metric learning, the SGTM-TT method builds upon the widely used Nonlinear Dimensionality Reduction (NDR) techniques to create a dynamic map that reflects the temporal development of data points. Unlike existing methods, SGTM-TT enables the creation of data representations that are not only responsive to temporal changes but also informed by prior knowledge in the form of constraints. As a result, it produces a representation that is both easy to interpret and responsive to temporal variations. Furthermore, a constrained variant of the SGTM-TT method, referred to as CSGTM-TT, has been developed to address the limitations of the SGTM-TT method by incorporating user-defined constraints during the optimization process. By doing so, the CSGTM-TT method offers greater flexibility and control over the resulting representation, enabling the incorporation of domain-specific information to create a more meaningful and interpretable data representation. In order to facilitate the practical application of the SGTM-TT and CSGTM-TT methods, the development of the R-based SGTM-TT package is described in detail. This package provides a user-friendly environment to create interactive 3D maps, offering a range of customization options to enhance the usability and understandability of the resulting representations. To demonstrate the efficacy of the SGTM-TT and CSGTM-TT methods, several case studies from diverse domains have been conducted. These studies demonstrate the potential of the SGTM-TT and CSGTM-TT methods to create responsive and domain-specific data representations that are both responsive and easy to interpret. As a result, the SGTM-TT method has shown promise as a versatile tool for multivariate time series analysis and exploration, while the CSGTM-TT method offers greater flexibility and control over the resulting representation to create a more meaningful and interpretable data representation. Reinforcement learning seeks to develop the most effective strategies in complex systems through trial and error, often at great cost.  To automate this costly process, researchers have been exploring methods to transfer knowledge from similar tasks to unfamiliar ones.  One promising approach, using prior experience to modify policy adjustments, has shown potential, although it requires extensive prior knowledge to generate a useful map.  In contrast, a more recent method, called Prior Experience Guided Policy (PEGP), uses prior knowledge to make policy adjustments based on the similarity between tasks, without needing a comprehensive map.  In this research, the PEGP method is applied to multiple reinforcement learning environments, including small-scale games and a simulated power system.  The results indicate that incorporating the PEGP method results in significantly fewer training episodes needed to achieve a high return rate.  Furthermore, when tested in unrelated power system planning tasks, the PEGP method allowed agents to produce optimal solutions more quickly, up to 3.7 times faster, while producing solutions with lower variance.  Overall, the PEGP method shows great promise for large-scale reinforcement learning applications in the future.  The code for this research is available online.  Additionally, this research was supported by a grant from the C3.ai Digital Transformation Knowledge Program. In video action detection, current research often relies on classifying actions based on localized spatiotemporal features. This paper examines a multi-stage game known as the cognitive hierarchy of best responses (CHBR) game. In this framework, players simultaneously belong to distinct cognitive hierarchies. We demonstrate that the CHBR game possesses well-defined, unique Nash equilibria that can be effectively computed through a variation of the iterative procedure used in the hierarchical Bayesian potential games framework. Our study finds that, under certain conditions, the CHBR game's Nash equilibria converge rapidly when players update their strategies according to a specific learning rule. Additionally, the analysis reveals that, relative to alternative models such as the hierarchical Bayesian potential games, the CHBR game facilitates more rapid learning and stronger welfare guarantees. We also present empirical evidence highlighting the distinct predictive capabilities of the CHBR game model when applied to actual game data. Finally, the analysis shows that, in scenarios featuring correlated types, the CHBR game's Nash equilibria exhibit striking robustness in the face of varying cognitive hierarchy parameters. Our study's findings suggest potential avenues for further research into the strategic behavior of players with diverse cognitive abilities and how their interactions might be influenced by factors such as differences in risk tolerance, information availability, and time constraints. We discuss how the CHBR game framework can be extended along these dimensions, leading to novel models like the risk hierarchy of best responses (RBR) and the time hierarchy of best responses (TBR) games. Our approach employs a general method for computing Nash equilibria in these extended game variants and demonstrates that they share similar learning dynamics and robustness properties as the CHBR game. Notably, the TBR game's Nash equilibria exhibit particularly robust responses to variations in the hierarchy parameter, suggesting potential applications in game-based tests of cognitive abilities and their links to neurological markers. Overall, the CHBR, RBR, and TBR models offer a unified framework for studying the strategic behavior of players across diverse cognitive and temporal characteristics, thereby enriching the understanding of decision-making processes. As such, these extended game variants possess broad applicability to various domains, encompassing both human and artificial agent populations. Moreover, the models can be adapted to accommodate mixed cognitive hierarchies and temporal characteristics, leading to novel models like the mixed cognitive hierarchy of best responses (MCHBR) and the mixed time hierarchy of best responses (MTBR) games. Our study shows that the MCHBR and MTBR games exhibit similar learning dynamics, robustness properties, and responses to parameter variations as their pure counterparts, the CHBR and TBR games, respectively. We propose a new understanding of object recognition that goes beyond just visual appearance. We believe that object recognition is an inherent part of video analysis and that accounting for object persistence between frames is essential for resolving multiple co-occurring objects. To test this idea, we've developed a pre-trained video transformer model that represents object persistence through an internal memory system. We've also created a new set of challenging video analysis tasks that require object recognition in complex scenarios, such as identifying multiple co-occurring objects, to measure our approach's effectiveness. We've seen that our method outperforms traditional object recognition methods on these tasks. We've also found that networks designed for image recognition often struggle with object persistence, whereas those designed for video analysis naturally account for it. Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models have become essential tools in both theoretical and application-based research, but existing algorithms used to learn these models' parameters often get stuck in local optima, particularly when the data distribution doesn't match the expected distribution over expert indices. To address this limitation, we've developed a novel, sample-efficient method for learning MoE models that always converges to a high-quality solution, even for complex, non-trivial cases. Unlike traditional algorithms, our approach can adapt to any data distribution and doesn't rely on pre-specified conditions or precomputed expert assignments. Instead, our method dynamically divides input indices into two groups, using only in-sample data: indices where experts agree and those where they don't agree. By clustering the agreed indices, we recover the MoE model, while assigning specific inputs to experts using only in-sample data. This approach is sample-efficient, as it requires a number of samples that grows slowly with problem size, remaining nearly the same for varying dimensions. Moreover, our method's sample efficiency is largely independent of the number of experts, making it highly scalable. To demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, we've successfully applied it to a range of tasks, including classification and density estimation, achieving state-of-the-art results with significantly reduced data requirements. For example, our method trained on just 1000 examples can outperform algorithms trained on 10,000 examples when dealing with a complex task. Overall, our method offers a highly efficient and adaptable solution for learning complex MoE models that can handle any data distribution. It provides a versatile approach that can be applied to a broad range of inductive biases, making it a highly transferable and universal learning technique. The reliability of a discrete-time channel model that relies on discrete, evenly spaced noise points is the focus. 
Initially, we establish that these noise points must be at minimum the normalized version of the eigenvalues of the channel's covariance matrix when attempting to accurately represent the channel's behavior. 
Conversely, we show that this noise pattern can effectively capture the channel's characteristics as long as the distance between these points surpasses the normalized version of the gap between the largest and smallest eigenvalues of the channel's covariance matrix. 
Furthermore, we propose a method to estimate the channel's memory based on this distance and present a lower-bound on this distance that is proportional to the channel's memory. 
Lastly, we investigate the effectiveness of interpolating between distinct noise points in order to obtain a precise channel representation. 
Our findings suggest that if the distance between these points is sufficiently high, the interpolated channel will converge to the exact channel impulse response. 
Notably, we demonstrate that even with a distance of one (i.e., a single noise point), the interpolated channel will accurately reconstruct the exact channel impulse response, despite being under-determined. 
Moreover, we show that this interpolation technique can be viewed as a form of spectral regularization. 
By applying this method to various types of channels, such as Gaussian and non-Gaussian channels, and MIMO channels, we are able to recover the exact channel characteristics. 
Our numerical experiments reveal that our proposed method can accurately identify the channel's memory even when the channel's covariance matrix contains a significant number of near-zero eigenvalues. 
Notably, our method can recover the exact channel memory at a distance of one (i.e., a single noise point) for all channels we tested, regardless of their type or properties. 
Our findings also indicate that the reliability of the channel model can be further enhanced by incorporating additional noise points. 
Consequently, our proposed method can be utilized as a general and robust channel identification technique applicable to a broad class of communication channels.

The widespread adoption of Android as the global leading operating system makes it an appealing target for malware. To counter this threat, security experts continuously develop advanced detection systems based on machine learning and deep learning. However, skilled hackers counter these systems by adapting their malware samples to avoid detection through a technique known as evasion attacks. This paper focuses on a specific type of evasion attack known as problem-space evasion attacks, where hackers modify Android malware to operate normally on the same device as the malware's intended behavior. Research on this topic is limited, so we're taking a comprehensive approach to analyze problem-space evasion attacks, including the types of such attacks, the characteristics of compromised devices, and the feasibility of such attacks. Our research suggests that problem-space evasion attacks are a serious concern, as existing detection systems are ineffective against such attacks, and the feasibility of such attacks increases significantly when the target device is also infected with the same type of malware. Our findings highlight the need for further research into this emerging threat, which poses a significant challenge to the effectiveness of mobile malware detection systems. This study addresses the strategic planning of ridepooling services in sprawling metropolises by developing a computational model to determine the optimal balance between pooling participation and customer diversion. In this context, pooling participation refers to the percentage of passengers who contribute to shared rides, while customer diversion represents the extent to which riders deviate from the most direct route to drop off friends en route. By analyzing the complex dynamics of urban mobility and market equilibrium, our model provides valuable insights into the interplay between over-supply and under-demand, as well as market segmentation. Furthermore, our results show that ridepooling service providers can mitigate both pooling under-supply and diversion by adjusting their pricing strategies in response to market conditions. This pricing policy involves setting lower prices during peak demand periods and higher prices during non-peak periods, which coincides with empirical observations of price dynamics in ridepooling markets. To illustrate the practical implications of our model, we apply it to four major cities in the United States and Europe and find that market conditions can be categorized into four segments, with pooling under-supply prevailing in non-peak hours and diversion occurring more frequently during peak hours. Notably, our study reveals that pooling under-supply tends to decrease over time, while diversion shows greater fluctuations, which are influenced by city-specific factors. This research contributes to our understanding of the complexities of ridepooling markets by identifying key factors and market conditions that affect participation and diversion rates. By quantifying the relative importance of factors like route detours and pooling contributions, we gain a deeper insight into the trade-offs that ridepooling service providers make when setting their prices and fares. Notably, our study reveals that pooling contributions generally exceed route detours in the United States, whereas in Europe, pooling contributions are lower than route detours. This research provides valuable guidance for ridepooling service providers to set their prices and fares effectively. By offering lower prices during peak hours when pooling contributions exceed route detours, service providers can attract more passengers. Conversely, they should charge higher prices during non-peak hours when pooling contributions are lower than route detours. Additionally, our study offers advice on fare structures, suggesting that flat fares are more suitable during peak hours, whereas two-tier pricing systems are more applicable during non-peak hours. Lastly, our study sheds light on the potential of ridepooling as a means of reducing urban air pollution by comparing the carbon dioxide emissions of shared and private rides. A significant function in most deep learning algorithms for brain imaging is brain segmentation, a crucial step in gathering data for further analysis like measuring brain volume. Researchers have utilized Unet-like architectures to segment the brain from magnetic resonance imaging scans, but these methods primarily rely on numerical data rather than the brain's structural patterns. To bridge this gap, we present DIM-Unet, a novel method that combines the strengths of Unet's efficient and robust segmentation capabilities with the brain's structural pattern knowledge gained through the Deep InfoMax training method. We thoroughly evaluate the efficacy of DIM-Unet by comparing it with other approaches in a multi-center, multi-ethnic cohort of children with brain tumors, as well as other automated and semi-automatic segmentation methods. Our results demonstrate that DIM-Unet achieves exceptional performance with an overall segmentation dice score of 0.8461, surpassing other approaches significantly. Additionally, we found that DIM-Unet's segmentation accuracy is consistent across various sub-regions and pathological conditions, with an accuracy of 0.8461, 0.7639, and 0.7539 for supratentorial, infratentorial, and non-tumor cerebral glioma sub-regions respectively. Notably, our approach outperforms even the most advanced automated methods, achieving accuracy in the range of 0.7541 to 0.8442 for the supratentorial, infratentorial, and non-tumor cerebral glioma sub-regions. Overall, our results indicate that DIM-Unet is a highly effective and reliable automated segmentation tool for brain tumor imaging. This study presents a comprehensive explanation of the I-score, a critical component in text classification tasks. The I-score determines which specific words drive a particular model's predictions by calculating their contribution to class membership. Building upon existing work, this research expands upon the I-score by accommodating complex sentence structures, incorporating the BERT language model, and accounting for irrelevant words. The proposed methodology is paired with a generative adversarial network-based word selection method. Experimental validation with the IMDB dataset demonstrates the effectiveness of the I-score in pinpointing crucial words for a model's prediction accuracy. Furthermore, integration of crucial words into a simple SVM classifier showcases improved performance compared to a baseline SVM on the same dataset. Finally, an analysis of the selected words highlights their semantic characteristics, offering insights into their potential usefulness in word embedding systems. The code and pre-trained models for this research can be accessed at the repository https://github.com/andrealexandry/I-score-BERT. This repository serves as a starting point for researchers to reproduce the findings and further enhance the I-score and accompanying methods. Additionally, a dataset containing the selected words for each class on the IMDB can be found at https://drive.google.com/drive/U/1P. The final objective is to enable other researchers to leverage the I-score and other methods presented in this work as a resource, facilitating improved results in information extraction tasks. The research aims to contribute to the field of linguistics by providing a tool for extracting meaningful linguistic patterns, ultimately aiding in the development of more efficient word embedding systems. Notably, our data suggest that there are six distinct rotational parameters associated with all-atom simulations involving nucleic acids, which can vary independently. We apply this protocol to manipulate an effective qubit, achievable with a quantum system exhibiting Stark-shifted degenerate states. The counterdiabatic protocol for such a system involves a specific, experimentally accessible driving potential based on two-level atoms. However, this driving potential lacks analytic expression due to its complexity and is only applicable in a specific, experimentally bounded parameter range. An alternative approach, utilizing a piecewise approximation of the driving potential, is proposed, demonstrating that the counterdiabatic state can be accurately achieved within this constrained domain using just three segments. We provide a general formula for computing the CD Hamiltonian and numerical evidence indicating high fidelity with only two segment approximations, suggesting the piecewise protocol may be more practical in experimental settings. Furthermore, the study showcases the versatility of the counterdiabatic protocol by achieving a full range of states (from ground state to maximally entangled) within a single, harmonic trap containing a single atom, simply by adjusting its peak amplitude and frequency. Ultimately, the piecewise protocol is proposed as a viable technique for experimental realization of the counterdiabatic method. As an added benefit, the study provides a general framework for assessing the protocol's performance in any given scenario, given a known CD Hamiltonian. We also explore the concept of optimal control, where the counterdiabatic protocol is used in a reverse manner to calculate the driving potential inducing target states. In this context, the counterdiabatic protocol is seen as an alternative optimal control method, potentially more robust against system errors, with the added benefit of being analytically computable in the case of the qubit system. Deep neural networks, known for their robust performance across various tasks, are often difficult to understand. This interpretability issue severely hampers their use in critical areas, like medical imaging. A promising approach to mitigate this is to develop model-agnostic interpretability methods. Specifically, visualizing deep neural network decisions through class feature spaces has significant value. However, creating such a space from an "M"-shaped classification prediction graph is an unsolved problem. Our novel method employs graph neural networks and a novel optimization technique based on hyperbolic geometry to efficiently generate a curved linear space that accurately represents a deep neural network's key characteristics. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method by showcasing its ability to seamlessly integrate existing interpretability methods, like feature importance visualizations, in a cohesive manner. Furthermore, our method's performance is comparable to or even superior to existing alternatives across multiple benchmarks, encompassing computer vision tasks and data sets (MNIST, CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100) as well as medical imaging (Barcelona Breast Density, Barrett's Esophagus). Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/0x0mar/hyperbolic-learn. 

Keywords: deep neural networks, interpretability, hyperbolic geometry, graph neural networks, medical imaging.

The geometrical Bohr-Mottelson model describes collective nuclear behavior, similar to a droplet, to understand nuclear structure below the shell model's energy threshold. This simple model helps us understand the general features of nuclear structure, particularly the energy spectrum's low-energy pattern. This note discusses the core principles of the BM model, focusing on the physical implications of the model's main parameters: surface thickness and a surface potential term, both of which are essential for mapping the single-particle potential. To achieve this, we modify the original Lagrangian, incorporating collective degrees of freedom and then apply the method of minimal length to derive the BM Hamiltonian. By doing so, we obtain new expressions for key BM parameters: surface thickness, and a vital term, essential for describing nuclear clustering, both of which are now expressed in terms of the minimal length parameter. This approach allows us to explore the physical effects of the minimal length on nuclear structure, a novel aspect of this work. To validate our model, we compare its predictions to the well-established nuclear data. Importantly, our model's predictions for the nuclear clustering, a long-standing issue in nuclear structure, are supported by the experimental data across the entire isotopic range, from stable to very neutron-rich nuclei. This work demonstrates how the minimal length parameter can be utilized to gain new insights into the novel nuclear structure, a long-standing challenge in this field. By doing so, we uncover the deep connection between the minimal length's quantum geometric effects and the geometric BM model's free parameters, a unique aspect of this work. We examine Neural Networks (NNs) as a solution for detecting and transcribing spoken language on resource-constrained Internet of Things (IoT) devices. By modifying a compact Neural Network to process audio in real-time, we can identify keywords and maintain a minimal memory footprint. Our analysis shows that using a Compact Neural Network results in a 43-fold reduction in storage requirements and a 27-fold decrease in computational resources compared to its fully connected counterpart. Additionally, we have developed a Spoken Language Dataset (SLD) to evaluate the performance of NN models on IoT devices. Using this dataset, we have determined the optimal Neural Network architecture for keyword spotting, consisting of 3 Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) layers with 3, 6, and 12 filters respectively, and a 64-unit Softmax layer. This architecture achieves an impressive accuracy of 97.3% and an accuracy of 96.3% when processing 20 words per second. Notably, this Neural Network design can operate on devices with as little as 128KB of RAM and a 32-bit processor. Moreover, we have successfully implemented and tested the CNN-based keyword spotting system on a range of popular IoT platforms, including the Contiki and Linux operating systems. Our findings indicate that Contiki OS exhibits superior performance due to its optimized memory allocation and communication stack. Notably, the Contiki OS exhibits a latency of 12ms and an energy consumption of 0.24mW, making it the preferred choice for IoT applications. Our research demonstrates that NN-based keyword spotting can be efficiently integrated with IoT devices and platforms, operating at the edge of the network. This enables real-time detection and processing of spoken language while conserving network bandwidth and storage resources. The model assumes the size of claims and portfolio dynamics for the insurer and reinsurer to be Markovian. The paper demonstrates that the best-response strategies for the insurer and reinsurer can be computed efficiently through resolution of variational inequalities, further establishing the existence and uniqueness of the most effective pure Nash equilibrium. Notably, our approach presents a pioneering attempt to tackle equilibrium selection among multiple candidate equilibria. To accomplish this, we introduce a distance metric between Nash equilibria based on the size of the set of feasible investment and reinsurance parameters. The method involves iteratively updating the insurer's and reinsurer portfolios until convergence is achieved, at which point the corresponding Markov control is realized as the best-response strategy for each player, ultimately enabling the determination of the optimal risk-sharing agreement between the insurer and reinsurer. The study supports its claims with numerical examples demonstrating the applicability of the model across a range of insurance contexts. The Compact Muon Solenoid (CMS) is one of the primary detectors in the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) at CERN, tracking particle interactions resulting from high-energy collisions. As part of the CMS system, the silicon pixel detector forms the innermost component responsible for navigating the trajectory of particles. Although initially operational between 2009 and 2016, it has been replaced with an upgraded variant in 2017. During a period of hiatus, the original detector experienced radiation damage equivalent to 136 radiation damage scale units (RDU), approximately one-third of its expected lifetime dose. This study examines the relationship between charge collection efficiency and hit efficiency in the context of radiation damage, utilizing data from the year 2011 as a reference point. Following the 2016 displacement and refurbishment, four new pixel detector modules, featuring embedded readout electronics, were field-tested during a proton-proton run in 2017. This research aims to investigate these modules' performance under real collision conditions. Furthermore, based on the measured charge collection efficiency, a predictive model for the hit efficiency of the updated pixel detector during proton-proton running has been established. This new model takes into account the level of radiation damage and operational voltage across each pixel's active area. Using the measured hit efficiency of the updated pixel detector during proton-proton running as a baseline, the study forecasts the hit efficiency of the updated pixel detector during heavy-ion running with enhanced radiation conditions. To investigate this, researchers examined the connection between the morphologies of 83 AGN host galaxies, identified through Hubble Space Telescope images, and their luminosity and black hole mass. The study revealed that larger, early-type galaxies are associated with more massive black holes, whereas late-type galaxies, especially those with disturbed morphologies, are found with lower masses. Notably, the data show a significant break in the black hole mass distribution at $\log M=7.7$, corresponding to $M_\odot$), with late-type galaxies generally having black holes below this threshold and early-type galaxies above. This finding could be the result of black hole growth being limited by the availability of fuel from star formation in late-type galaxies. Alternatively, the data may indicate that black holes in early-type galaxies have already completed their growth phase and are now less fuel-intensive. The study's implications for black hole growth and evolution will be explored in more detail. The effect of nuclear short-range correlations on the kinetic energy of nuclei was analyzed using two distinct approaches. The first approach relied on the energy-dependent G matrix formalism, while the second approach utilized the mean-field approximation with the M\"unchner potential. The correlation effect on the kinetic energy was found to be minimal, at approximately 3 percent, and did not significantly differ between the two methods investigated. As such, it was concluded that the kinetic energy of nuclei can be accurately determined without needing to account for the intricate short-range correlations present in the nucleus. Therefore, a simple and effective energy scaling, proportional to A/3, was sufficient to obtain a good estimate of the kinetic energy in medium-sized nuclei. This simple scaling is expected to be useful in a wide range of scientific and engineering applications where nuclear materials are being utilized. The total binding energy of nuclei, however, does exhibit a notable sensitivity to the short-range correlations present, with predictions from the two methods diverging by about 5 percent. The significance of these correlations in determining the total binding energy of nuclei should not be overlooked. The findings from this study may have a substantial impact on the accuracy of a variety of scientific and engineering simulations utilizing nuclear materials as input parameters. The predicted accuracy of scaling the kinetic energy may be useful in a wide range of scientific and engineering applications such as materials science, chemistry, biology, and physics. The predicted binding energies of magic nuclei may also be useful in determining the total binding energy of nuclei. The non-linear QCD evolution equations ultimately lead to a saturation point where the momentum transfer exceeds the average distance between color charged constituents. As a result, the non-linear effects become sufficiently large and the momentum transfer exceeds the average inter-parton distance. In deep inelastic scattering or high-energy physical processes, the presence of a saturation momentum sets a boundary beyond which the usual perturbative QCD calculations break down. To gain insights into saturation momentum values, we examine two case studies: Drell-Yan transverse momentum distributions and electron-proton deep inelastic scattering, both of which are being measured with increased precision. We compare the accuracy of various saturation momentum estimates, including those derived from baryon and photon invariants, to the values obtained from microscopic calculations. In the process, the complexity of calculating physical quantities from microscopic saturation momentum values becomes apparent, and the limitations of the current toolkit for achieving such calculations from first principles are identified. Ultimately, the necessity for further advancements in large $x$ parton distribution functions and gluon saturation physics is highlighted. To facilitate progress in this area, the current status of the field and open challenges and future research directions are outlined. In particular, the potential contributions of lattice QCD and new experimental initiatives aimed at bridging the current theoretical limitations are discussed. In conclusion, the potential for significant breakthroughs in our understanding of the gluon distribution function and saturation physics is identified. Furthermore, the potential applications of saturation physics research findings, including their relevance to hadron-hadron collisions, are examined and discussed. To begin addressing these applications, an analysis of the current status of saturation physics in hadron-hadron collisions is provided, along with a discussion of future research directions and potential avenues for further exploration. In particular, the role of $k_T$-factorization and the challenges of achieving a precise description of single-inclusive quantities, such as transverse momentum distributions, are examined. Ultimately, the necessity for more precise saturation momentum values and a deeper understanding of the constraints on parton distribution functions and collision system complexity is highlighted, along with the potential contributions of new experimental initiatives aimed at bridging the current theoretical limitations. In particular, the potential applications of electron-ion collisions, where large $x$ parton distribution functions can be accessed with increased precision via the JLab 12 GeV beam energy upgrade, are discussed, along with the potential applications of proton-leading proton collisions, where the high multiplicity of final state particles can serve as a probe of the QCD saturation momentum. We examined the abundance of 10 elements within 398 metal-poor subgiant stars using detailed analysis, applying the most recent atomic data to calculate precise abundance measurements. Our results show a low intrinsic scatter among these stars in specific abundance ratios, ranging between 0.04-0.16 dex. This variation is primarily attributed to varying levels of enhanced elements rather than changes in metallicity. A low scatter was also found in the case of [Fe/H], indicating minimal star-to-star variation with an RMS intrinsic scatter of 0.06 dex. However, our findings show that [Fe/H] values determined from cross-correlation techniques may be overestimated due to the increased sensitivity to low-frequency variations. To correct for this issue, a weighted average should be obtained from multiple measurements to reduce the influence of these variations. Additionally, our analysis highlights the importance of utilizing the most recent atomic data for accurate abundance calculations. Using synthetic spectra based on updated atomic data can help minimize the abundance errors associated with atomic data uncertainties. Furthermore, our results suggest that hyperfine structure plays a significant role in measuring [Fe I]/[H] abundance ratios, particularly in cases where the electron density is low. Employing synthetic spectra that account for hyperfine structure can correct for associated errors and provide accurate abundance measurements. Utilizing a machine learning approach, we developed an automated system to evaluate atomic data, HF structures, and line profile parameters for accurate abundance calculations. This algorithm is expected to contribute positively to future studies to ensure the reliable determination of accurate abundance calculations. Using our dataset, we employed the Gaussian Process method to develop a regression model that can accurately predict [Fe/H] using a single line measurement, yielding a low RMS intrinsic scatter of 0.06 dex. This suggests that incorporating machine learning techniques can enhance the recovery of accurate [Fe/H] values from cross-correlation profiles and, to a greater extent, from spectroscopic measurements. Our results have significant implications for future studies to utilize machine learning and automated processes to ensure accurate and precise abundance calculations. Applying our dataset to training and testing models, we found that training on larger datasets results in lower intrinsic scatter and greater accuracy, while testing on different populations yields consistent results. Our study demonstrates the potential for machine learning to streamline and accelerate the determination of accurate abundance calculations, particularly for [Fe/H], to facilitate reliable recovery from cross-correlation profiles and, to a greater extent, from spectroscopic measurements. A novel machine learning approach has been developed that identifies and measures
the potential biases introduced by unobserved variables, which may nonetheless
influence predictions. This methodology is built on theoretical research which
establishes a quantitative framework for assessing the impact of missing
covariates on predictive models. As a result, a method is created that
automatically detects potential issues and provides a measurable assessment of
their overall influence. This methodology can be applied to multiple machine
learning models, including decision trees, kernel Ridge Regression, support
vector machines, deep neural networks, and more. Our approach is demonstrated
through its use in real-world datasets, which reveal the significant impact of
neglected variables on predictive accuracy, prediction uncertainty, and the
reliability of predictive models. By addressing these biases, our method
enables the enhancement of predictive performance, empirical reliability, and the
provision of accurate predictive surrogates. The implementation of this
methodology is facilitated through the open-source library BiasMachine. This
library provides a versatile interface for machine learning tasks and includes a
range of algorithms, including support for both batch and active learning. It
further incorporates data augmentation, regularization techniques, adversarial
training, and automated bias detection and measurement. With BiasMachine, users
can easily incorporate bias analysis into their machine learning workflows,
utilizing pre-trained models and incorporating their expertise through
user-defined callbacks. This enables the adaptation of models to new, unseen data
domains, as well as the identification of critical covariates and domain
characteristics. Furthermore, BiasMachine's active learning capabilities allow
users to efficiently explore new data domains with minimal new data collection
requirements. The full implementation is available on GitHub at
https://github.com/olgavalsari/biasmachine. This research is a part of the
thesis titled "Quantifying and Mitigating Bias in Machine Learning Models" and
is based on prior research including "Quantifying and Mitigating Bias in Machine
Learning" and "BAM! An Active Learning Framework for Exploring New Data
Domains". While these studies laid the theoretical groundwork for bias analysis,
the current research expands on those findings to develop a practical
implementation of bias analysis and provides a publicly available library.

Our algorithm combines a quantum random access memory-driven, gradient-descent based optimization technique to learn the parameters of a neural network with an embedded quantum circuit, along with a classical neural network used for reference purposes. The output of the quantum circuit serves as input to the reference network, whose prediction is then compared to the actual label through a loss function. By utilizing the reference network's predictions, we've adapted the classical gradient-descent method for simultaneous learning of the quantum circuit's parameters. Researchers, Chen and Garay, have previously studied pointwise slant submanifolds in almost Hermitian manifolds. We extend their work, investigating imbedded (not necessarily Isometric) pointwise slant submanifolds in complex space forms. Our research finds new conditions for these submanifolds to be totally geodesic or minimal, as well as principles that ensure proper immersion. Additionally, we establish a maximum bound on the first Betti number for pointwise slant submanifolds that are not totally geodesic. Furthermore, we examine a key case where the submanifold meets a specific condition related to its structure, obtaining several important theorems and identifying a need for further research in this area. Lastly, we present a regression model aimed at predicting three-dimensional shapes of pointwise slant submanifolds in complex space forms. Our model utilizes multivariate scalar fields as input and predicts three-dimensional surfaces as output. Notably, this model can predict both new and existing shapes of these submanifolds. Our research found that, on a given complex space form, 90% of 1000 randomly selected 3D surfaces of the torus were actual or nearly pointwise slant submanifolds. Our findings suggest the potential for further research in machine learning applied to geometry. Ultimately, our research contributes five new papers related to this topic. In the rapidly evolving field of epidemiology, researchers are developing various mathematical frameworks to analyze the spread of contagious diseases and assess the effectiveness of control measures. A novel model presented in this work builds on the SIS model by initially grouping individuals into distinct clusters, whose movements are fixed, and then allowing for temporary temporary exchanges between them. The analysis commences with a small number of active infections within a single cluster and explores the potential for containing the outbreak within it, or spreading it to other clusters, given the constraints of stay-at-home orders. The model also considers the dynamic movement of individuals, influenced by a non-degenerate covariance matrix that describes random group transitions. The initial phase of the epidemic in each cluster is characterized by an explosive early spread, and the critical threshold for when the outbreak escapes the initial cluster is identified. The model's critical parameters are estimated from recent US COVID-19 data and preliminary epidemiological estimates, and the implications of these findings are discussed in the context of stay-at-home orders effectiveness. Furthermore, numerical simulations are conducted to illustrate the model's predictions, and an approximation technique is developed to facilitate efficient computation of the epidemic's time evolution. The model's versatility is demonstrated by showing that specific limiting cases recover key aspects of established epidemiological models. The findings suggest that stay-at-home orders may hinder an outbreak from spreading beyond its initial scope, but only if certain conditions are met and the initial infection count is kept low. The model has the potential to be expanded to analyze the effects of vaccines and other control measures. Future research directions, such as generalizing the model to account for varying group sizes, are also explored. The accompanying code and model source can be accessed at https://github.com/asharoo90/cluster_model. Additionally, a brief tutorial outlining the model's usage can be found at https://github.com/asharoo90/cluster_model/blob/master/tutorials/tut1.md. A related PhD dissertation can be found at https://repository.lib.fit.edu/islandora/object/FIT%3A1071.

Interpreting teaching content is a complex process that can be easily disrupted by misunderstandings in the teacher-student communication channel. In particular, referential confusion arises when multiple objects are identified by the same label in a teaching content, causing different ambiguities among the teacher and student. While the teacher knows the intended focus, the student is left to deduce the correct reference solely based on the content's linguistic cues. As a result, even with perfect content interpretation, the learner may still encounter significant interpretation challenges. Our study examines the extent to which the content's structure can facilitate the learner's interpretation and reduce referential confusion. We propose that both semantic and structural aspects of the content can aid the learner in resolving ambiguity. Our research involves an empirical study of the effects of semantic and structural cues on the learner's interpretation of referential ambiguity in educational content using a crowd-sourced dataset. Our results indicate that adding structural information can alleviate referential confusion and provide insights for designing effective educational content to minimize ambiguity and enhance the teacher-student communication channel. Our findings also highlight the significance of the content's structure in overcoming referential confusion and offer practical implications for creating unambiguous content. Furthermore, our study demonstrates the potential of using human annotations to improve the content's interpretability and reduce ambiguity, ultimately improving the teacher-student communication channel. Our research contributes to the field by providing a clear understanding of the causes of interpretation difficulties and suggesting potential solutions to minimize referential confusion and improve the content's interpretability. Our study also showcases the potential of using human annotations to improve the content's structure and reduce ambiguity, ultimately improving the teacher-student communication channel. Our research findings can be applied to other areas of machine learning, such as generative models, by identifying the types of interpretation difficulties that can arise and developing methods to mitigate them. Accurate understanding of quantum systems is essential for reliable quantum computing and sensing.  Quantum process tomography, a method for fully characterizing quantum processes, is crucial but often impractical due to its typically exponential time complexity.  A newly developed efficient quantum process estimation approach reaches optimal sampling efficiency, outperforming previous methods.  By transforming the estimation problem into a probability distribution fitting task and employing Poisson's equation solution techniques, the proposed algorithm achieves a significant time reduction compared to previous solutions.  A practical implementation of this method on real-world data showcases its ability to achieve state-of-the-art results with significantly reduced resources.  The proposed solution is modular, flexible, and suitable for a wide range of quantum systems, making it a valuable tool for a variety of applications.  A related open-source code repository is available for further research and development at \url{https://github.com/QuantumSensing/quantum-process-estimation}.  The research demonstrates the ability to obtain precise estimates of multi-qubit quantum systems with high accuracy, opening new avenues for the application of quantum sensing and computing.  The study also highlights the development of novel machine learning algorithms capable of processing real-time data from quantum devices, a crucial requirement for the reliable deployment of quantum devices in real-world settings. The discovery of a Hubble tension exists between early universe and late universe models of cosmic expansion.  Stochastic gravitational-wave backgrounds (SGWbs) could resolve this discrepancy by modifying the expansion history.  We investigated the impact of SGWs on the expansion history using a variable deceleration parameter approach.  We derived a mathematical equation based on this parameter's definition and applied it to constrain the growth rate and characteristic frequencies of SGWs using Cosmic Microwave Background data.  Additionally, we used this variable deceleration parameter to reanalyze the redshift drift constraint and found that existing SGW models fail to resolve the Hubble tension.  However, our findings suggest that future observations of low-frequency SGWs could still be detectable using next-generation cosmic clock experiments.  These experiments could potentially detect SGWs with frequencies as low as 10^-14 Hz using improved precision levels, which is an order of magnitude better than current SGW detection capabilities.  As a result, future experiments could theoretically detect SGWs just 10% of the age of the universe away from today.  This could significantly expand our understanding of the universe's early stages.  Importantly, our analysis demonstrates that existing cosmic clock experiments are already close to reaching the theoretical detection threshold for SGWs. We propose an unsupervised speech synthesis approach consisting of two key elements: a flexible text processing system and a voice editing framework. Our text processing system enables accurate text-to-speech alignment without pre-existing transcripts, and can be utilized in conjunction with any existing speech synthesis technique. Conversely, our voice editing framework is self-sufficient and doesn't rely on pre-existing voices. It employs a innovative method for voice comparison and a voice manipulation technique called voice blending. This approach is illustrated through its application in a pioneering study where we teach a text-to-speech model to read in the language of its original articulation, thereby overcoming its initial pronunciation deficiencies. Our voice editing framework is further validated by producing novel voices for a target language using only non-target language audio examples. When paired with a text processor, these edited voices can be combined to produce high-quality, natural-sounding synthesized speech in the target language. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach through a synthesis example where our system correctly pronounces Chinese characters despite initially being trained on only Japanese text and audio. Ultimately, this research represents a significant step towards creating speech synthesis systems without pre-defined voices or language data. The accompanying code and audio samples can be accessed via https://github.com/Hiromu-T/Unsupervised-Speech-Synthesis.

The Dynaswap project is focused on developing a robust, trustworthy architecture for safeguarding complex cyberinfrastructures against cyber threats. Aspect-based sentiment analysis focuses on determining the sentiment of a particular aspect within product reviews. Normally, reviews contain explicit opinions such as "I like the camera's quality." However, reviews can also convey implicit sentiment without explicitly stating it, like through compliments or faults implied by a lack of criticism. Despite this, current research largely overlooks implicit sentiment in reviews. To address this, we propose a model called LSPE, which incorporates two key components: one identifies and classifies explicit and implicit sentiment, and the other determines the sentiment of a specified aspect based on the identified sentiment. We conduct experiments on the NABANK and NALIM datasets and achieve top results in both explicit and implicit sentiment classification, as well as overall aspect-based sentiment analysis. We also release our code on the GitHub platform for public access. Furthermore, we release a new dataset, the IMPLICIT-SEM, which contains implicit sentiment semantics extracted from product reviews, to facilitate further research. The hope is that our work will stimulate future studies on implicit sentiment analysis. Researchers have long debated how deep neural networks process language by parsing it into multiple levels, including syntax, semantics, and pragmatics. A prevailing joint modeling approach suggests that these levels are interconnected and that a single model can capture them simultaneously, leading to superior performance. This study challenges this notion by investigating whether distinct models for syntax and semantics can achieve comparable results when trained in tandem. We draw on theories from cognitive psychology and linguistic expertise to inform our analysis, positing that these complex tasks require a deeper understanding than can be conveyed through fine-tuning with gradient descent alone. Our findings support this claim, demonstrating that separate models for syntax and semantics trained together with a controller model achieve results on par with joint models across various parsing tasks, including those for SQuAD and Kosaka datasets. Additionally, our results show that a simple averaging method suffices to synthesize outputs from multiple models as effectively as joint models. Ultimately, our research highlights the need for a deeper examination of the role of optimization methods in natural language processing. In 2015, CERN introduced "Emittance Scans," a cutting-edge luminosity calibration method, which has been successfully implemented at the Large Hadron Collider since 2017, with the start of Run 2. This innovative approach has significantly reduced reliance on sensitive and prone to fatigue "beam cleaning scans," by instead relying on stable, high-intensity beam conditions. Run 2 saw the continuous development and refinement of emittance scans in numerous beam configurations, including proton and lead-ion beams. This paper details the evolution of emittance scans, documenting improvements made between 2016 and 2017, as well as their widespread application across various LHC experiments. Data from the ATLAS and CMS collaborations demonstrate the accuracy of luminosity measurements using emittance scans, with results comparable to those obtained through other calibration methods. This precision enables the precise determination of the LHC's luminosity, with an accuracy of 1.4% for proton beams and 3% for heavy ion beams, when using emittance scans in isolation. This development has opened up new possibilities for precision luminosity calibration and has paved the way for the determination of precise luminosity measurements during high-energy physics experiments at the LHC. Furthermore, the versatility of this method allows it to be adapted for use in other future high-energy colliders. 

Keywords: LHC, Emittance Scans, Luminosity Calibration, Run 2, LHC.

Recent breakthroughs in artificial neural networks have accelerated the growth of data science, and artificial intelligence. However, a significant challenge remains in the ability of these networks to continuously adapt to new tasks without forgetting previously learned skills. This phenomenon of catastrophic forgetting is particularly prevalent when neural networks are tasked with processing data from different distributions. Various approaches have been proposed to mitigate this issue, including the use of low capacity networks, replaying previous data, and techniques such as knowledge distillation and pseudo-rehearsal. This survey aims to provide a comprehensive overview of the current state of the field, with a particular focus on the computational aspects and experimental evaluations. It also identifies key challenges and potential research directions that need to be addressed in order to make neural networks more resilient to catastrophic forgetting. One of the primary hurdles that still needs to be overcome is the development of domain-invariant features that can help decouple task-specific and domain-specific knowledge. This approach has shown promise in semi-supervised learning domains, but a more comprehensive understanding of the relationship between domain shifts and neural networks' representations is still needed. Ultimately, the development of robust neural networks that can learn and adapt continuously in real-world applications remains a pressing issue, and a deeper computational understanding of the problem is essential for its effective solution. Verifying facts using structured data can be difficult, as it demands not only identifying relevant information but also accurately comparing it to the stated claim. In this project, we address this challenge by proposing a new technique for structured data verification. Initially, we pre-process and encode both the claim and data into a suitable format suitable for analysis by existing verification models. Our method then relies on pre-trained natural language understanding models to perform claim verification tasks. In order to accelerate verification tasks involving large datasets, we pre-train these encoders on a substantial training set, thereby enabling efficient verification of new claims. Our approach, which we call StructDataVerify, exhibits exceptional performance on benchmark datasets, outperforming current best methods by significant margins when resources are constrained. For instance, when processing the FactCheck.fm dataset with a 128 GPU cluster for just 2 hours, StructDataVerify achieves an impressive F1 score of 0.7146, thereby establishing a new benchmark for verification tasks involving structured data. Our implementation of StructDataVerify is publicly available at https://github.com/allan-zhou/StructDataVerify. We've developed Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) and maximum a posteriori (MAP) methods for estimating the parameters of a Bayesian probabilistic model of uncertainty quantification. This model is based on a complex system with stochastic thresholds and can be applied to a wide range of problems, including the stochastic three-dimensional Brusselator model. Due to its high dimensionality, efficient numerical simulation is challenging, but our Bayesian approach allows for accurate inference of the system's parameters under uncertain conditions. However, the computational cost of the MCMC and MAP methods grows exponentially with the number of stochastic parameters, making them impractically slow for large dimensions. We overcome this issue by employing differential evolution algorithms, which significantly accelerate the MCMC and MAP processes by at least one order of magnitude, even in the case of 100 stochastic parameters. We also explore the feasibility of parallelizing the MAP method using graphics processing units (GPUs), but find that the MCMC method with differential evolution outperforms the MAP method with GPU parallelization due to its lower overhead and greater degree of parallelizability. Overall, our research demonstrates the utility of Bayesian uncertainty quantification for the three-dimensional Brusselator model and highlights the importance of efficient numerical simulation. With the aid of the MCMC and MAP methods, we are able to achieve precise accuracy in the uncertainty quantification of the model's mean and variance. Furthermore, our results show that the MCMC method is more stable than the MAP method in scenarios with poorly informed prior distributions. We also investigate the impact of stochastic parameters on the model's mean and variance, revealing that the model's stochasticity has a considerable effect on its average concentration. Notably, our research provides valuable insights into the uncertainty quantification of the model's mean and variance across various dimensions, showing that the MCMC method exhibits a cross-over phenomenon in computational time as the number of dimensions increases. When the number of dimensions is low (less than 20), the MCMC method is faster than the MAP method, but as the number of dimensions grows (greater than 50), the MCMC method becomes significantly slower. We attribute this unusual behavior to the efficient initial phase of the MCMC method, during which the algorithm samples the posterior distribution quickly and accurately, but as the number of dimensions continues to grow, the MCMC method becomes increasingly inefficient. Overall, our research demonstrates the utility and efficiency of the MCMC and MAP methods in the uncertainty quantification of the Bayesian probabilistic model

A critical consideration when employing deep learning in medical imaging is identifying when data is inconsistent with the training set's characteristics. This problem is particularly pressing because these tasks often result in unpredictable outcomes if patients outside the initial data collection specifications are subsequently included. Therefore, developing effective out-of-distribution detection methods is essential. In this research, we present a unified framework that integrates out-of-distribution detection, data training, and model training into an interconnected unit, which is optimized collectively in relation to a unified loss function. Our proposed framework is versatile and can be applied to a variety of challenges including data training, out-of-distribution detection, and model training. Specifically, we demonstrate its utility in enhancing the accuracy of segmentation tasks involving rare medical conditions, such as retinal telangiectatic disease. Our results show that incorporating out-of-distribution detection capabilities leads to improved segmentation performance on publicly available datasets. On the same datasets, out-of-distribution detection performance is consistently high, with an area under the ROC curve exceeding 0.95 in most cases. Our research implementation is available online at https://github.com/alexs98/ODD Seg. This work was supported by the National Eye Institute of the National Institutes of Health through Grant R01EY028204.

As alternative methods for timekeeping become more prominent, such as using photon counting or reading Josiah Willard Gibbs' 'logical clock' based on Brownian motion, the traditional approach of designing clocks based on periodic oscillators may soon be surpassed. The exploration of non-periodic mechanisms for building clocks is, therefore, becoming increasingly significant. This research paper outlines a comprehensive theoretical framework for designing non-repeating clocks, specifically those driven by stochastic processes. It showcases a practical example - the dual pulse rate process - which serves as a model for a non-repeating clock. This example features a delicate balance between stochastic and deterministic behavior, characterized by a singular point, where the stochastic system closely mimics a deterministic one, resulting in highly accurate timekeeping. This clock design offers several key benefits, including the ability to start and stop the clock without disrupting it, as well as adjust its accuracy and scale, all without altering the clock mechanism itself. The potential for building accurate and stable clocks from non-repeating processes could have a significant impact on both physical timekeeping and the broader understanding of time. Finally, this research paper discusses how these non-repeating clocks relate to Gibbs' logical clock, revealing insights into the former's design parameters and the former's accuracy and scale constraints. It also provides insights into the former's design parameters and the former’s constraints. To facilitate further research into non-repeating clocks, this paper includes a supplementary section outlining potential experimental implementations of these systems. These non-repeating clocks, therefore, represent a new and innovative approach to timekeeping, one that is poised to revolutionize both physical timekeeping and the understanding of time. The results demonstrate the benefits of the GP noise model in accurately modeling the stochastic behavior of these load responses, and the GP scaling model effectively captures the hierarchical structure of noise dynamics without disregarding the coarser-scale met-codes' noise. In such cases, we determine the $R_\infty$-property for finite solvable groups of prime power order, establishing a characterization based on the group's $p$-part and the divisor of the group's order when the $p$-part is fixed. This characterization leads to a general characterization. Our study also covers the finiteness of twisted conjugacy classes in automorphisms of finite solvable groups. A characterization of the finiteness of these classes is given for groups of prime power order, with the group's $p$-part and the group order as parameters. This leads to a comprehensive characterization, with the group order as the sole parameter. Our results are illustrated with various examples. Furthermore, we introduce a concept of 'weak $R_\infty$-property' for automorphisms, resulting in additional characterizations of metabelian groups of this property, along with a description of the associated twisted conjugacy classes. This yields a characterization of the quasireflection automorphisms in metabelian groups. In particular, we find that a quasireflection in a metabelian group is an $R_\infty$-automorphism or an $R_\infty$-quasireflection based on the prime factorization of the group's order. This discovery enables a comprehensive characterization of quasireflection automorphisms in metabelian groups. Our analysis also covers the properties of non-quasireflection automorphisms in metabelian groups, resulting in a characterization of their existence and properties based on the group's order. Our study further explores the properties of non-quasireflection automorphisms in rank one nilpotent groups of class two, with the group order as the sole parameter. In particular, we find that such a non-quasireflection automorphism $\varphi$ results in an odd number of twisted conjugacy classes if and only if it exchanges the two generators of the group, defining a nilpotent group of class two. This condition, along with the properties of the exponent $e$ of the group, yields a comprehensive characterization of the non-quasireflection automorphisms in such groups, along with a description of their behavior based on the exponent and the number of elements in the quotient group formed by the exponent. In connection with the information paradox problem, theories such as BCFT and ICFT have been developed as a way to study null subspaces in AdS spaces. This paper builds on those developments by defining reflected entropy in BCFT and showing it has a dual interpretation in AdS. Specifically, it is proposed that the reflected entropy corresponds to the boundary a dual to the entanglement wedge cross section a half-way across from the entanglement wedge to the wedge itself. This claim is supported by examining the reflected entropy of a semi-infinite line in semi-chiral CFT, which is found to be 0. However, when considering holographic scenarios, where we use BCFT to model null boundaries within AdS spaces, the proposed dual interpretation is more complex. Nonetheless, when taking a specific limit, it is found that the reflected entropy is linearly proportional to the boundary a, indicating a relationship to information theory. Furthermore, it is observed that the rate of information transfer in this process is bounded by the holographic bound. These results are verified using an example of a quasi-chiral entanglement wedge in 3D AdS space. Recent uses of machine learning in algebraic geometry and physics are explored,  
revealing how an initial exercise in machine learning research can be resolved  
through a combination of established algebraic geometry and physics methodologies.  
Two primary cases are presented: the first involves employing deep learning to  
find decompositions of a given projective space into a product of lower  
dimensional projective spaces; the second utilizes reinforcement learning to locate  
points on moduli spaces, specifically within the linear system of forms of a  
given degree on a given algebraic surface. Within these examples, both the  
underlying mathematics and the related algorithms are examined, along with  
suggested improvements that could further accelerate learning speeds and introduce  
more sophisticated algorithms based on techniques such as neural networks and  
parametric tautological algebraic geometry. This work aims to demonstrate  
that machine learning research can benefit both the machine learning and algebraic  
geometry and physics communities by exchanging and consolidating ideas.  
Furthermore, discussions of open questions within the framework of this approach  
are presented, potentially guiding future research efforts.  
A significant portion of the work relies on an open-source Python code, freely  
accessible and distributable via GitHub at https://github.com/AMatheus1/Learning-Algebraic-Geometry.  
Furthermore, corresponding open issues have been posted on that platform,  
encouraging contributions from the machine learning and algebraic geometry/physics  
communities to address the presented challenges and deepens the interplay  
between these areas of research.  
A supplementary document is available at https://arxiv.org/abs/2202.10267,  
containing detailed descriptions of the code's functionality as well as the  
mathematical and computational outcomes achieved with this tool.
