Preemptive wildfire detection is vital for minimizing ecological damage, reducing fire spread, and saving lives. Unchecked wildfires can have disastrous consequences, and therefore, prompt and accurate fire detection is a top priority. This study presents an innovative fire detection algorithm, designed to identify wildfires in real-time by analyzing data from low-cost IoT sensors located throughout a specified area. The algorithm's core lies in a machine learning model, specifically a Support Vector Machine (SVM), which determines the likelihood of a wildfire based on the dynamic temperature readings from the sensors. To refine the detection process, an experimental approach involves simulating fires in a controlled environment and recreating real-world sensor data under various conditions. This ground-breaking approach enables the development of a scalable and efficient fire detection system, which can be scaled up to monitor large areas and effectively detect fires in dense or hard-to-reach areas. The results of the experiment reveal that the SVM model achieves remarkable accuracy, successfully detecting simulated fires in under 1 second and demonstrating an impressive false positive rate of less than 2% when operating at peak efficiency. This pioneering work sets the stage for the widespread adoption of IoT technology in large-scale environmental monitoring and intelligent sensing applications. The proposed system is poised to revolutionize the field of intelligent sensing, enabling the effective detection of not only wildfires but also other critical events such as landslides, floods, and more. The successful integration of the SVM model and real-time temperature data from IoT sensors marks a significant breakthrough in event detection and real-time monitoring. The study's findings serve as a foundation for future research to expand the scope of event detection to a broader range of situations. Furthermore, the presented algorithm and system offer an adaptable solution, suitable for deployment in a variety of real-world scenarios, and the experimental setup can be easily replicated in various settings to facilitate replication and enable cross-validation of the results across different environments and conditions. The open-access repository containing the complete experimental setup and sensor data enables researchers to validate the results, reproduce the study, and build upon the foundation established in this work. The dataset, which comprises 1,440 samples and 120 sequences per class, is specifically tailored to accommodate SVM-based algorithms and facilitates efficient model training and cross-validation. The repository is accessible at: https://github.com/asharakep/multi-class_svm_fire_detection. The collaboration of researchers in replicating the study is highly encouraged, and the use of the dataset is subject to a permissive Creative Commons Zero (CC0) policy, allowing researchers to utilize the dataset without restrictions.

However, identifying depression-specific content on social media platforms is challenging due to the lack of labeled data and difficulty in filtering relevant information.  To address this issue, we have created a dataset of non-professional language that is relevant to depression.  The dataset is divided into three categories of depression: mild, moderate, and severe symptoms.  Each category is distinct and characterized by specific mental health symptoms and treatments.  The dataset consists of 8,461 unique Instagram posts from 1,536 users and is marked using a novel labeling technique.  The dataset is available for public access at https://doi.org/10.21227/M7D8D.  We have also conducted a series of experiments to demonstrate the effectiveness of training a depression classifier using this dataset.  The study reveals that depression can be accurately identified from social media posts, and there are distinct patterns that set mild, moderate, and severe depression apart.  Furthermore, we have found that depression-specific content can be gathered in large quantities using simple search queries on social media platforms.  The study highlights the feasibility and potential of using social media platforms to support depression diagnosis and treatment. By simulating the model within Gaussian white noise, we derived a stochastic differential equation representation that allows us to estimate parameters based on COVID-19 reported data in Portugal. Findings indicate that Coronavirus cases in Portugal were initially increasing due to human error but then declined after lockdown measures were implemented in March 2020. Our model suggests that removing lockdown measures too early would lead to an increase in infections. Lockdown effectiveness varies across regions, and integrated simulation results reveal that lockdown measures have a greater impact when mortality rates are higher and the infection duration is longer. Furthermore, we observed that mortality rates in Portugal are significantly influenced by the Coronavirus, contradicting an initial report by the Portuguese authorities. These findings highlight the importance and urgency of continuing lockdown measures to mitigate the pandemic's severity. They also emphasize the need for unique lockdown strategies tailored to different regions, considering their distinct infection characteristics. Based on Portugal's infection data, we recommend a lockdown duration of at least 14 days for that country. Low-rank matrix recovery issues with complex high-dimensional data are widespread in both machine learning and signal processing. This work presents a family of robust tensor nuclear norm minimization problems addressing these problems. In many cases, data is segmented into multiple components, each observed under distinct conditions such as differing noise levels or sensor types. The proposed methods leverage the nuclear norm of a low-rank tensor matrix to reconstruct missing data segments. The paper provides a detailed derivation of the TNNM problem, along with a customized splitting algorithm for its solution. The method's effectiveness is demonstrated through theoretical guarantees and experimental results on synthetic and real-world datasets. These show the TNNM problem outperforms existing state-of-the-art techniques in both simplicity and recovery performance. Furthermore, its application to image super-resolution with multi-image data yields superior outcomes to current methods. Due to broken geometric symmetry, this system exhibits unique characteristics, such as "exceptional points" in the eigenvalue spectrum, where two energies cross and become identical, yielding non-Hermitian characteristics. Utilizing a simplified model as a starting point, we develop a more comprehensive Hamiltonian for the system, deriving a set of coupled, exact equations for the eigenstates, which we subsequently solve to analyze the eigenvalues and eigenfunctions. To distinguish between transverse and longitudinal vibrations, we introduce specific degrees of freedom and corresponding constraints. As the primary aspects of this system's behavior are governed by a single parameter, representing the ratio of one degree of freedom to the others, we use this parameter to create a 2D "phase diagram" that illustrates the system's characteristics for low and high values of this parameter. Additionally, we investigate how the presence of repulsive interactions between particles affects the system's characteristics, observing changes in energy splittings and eigenstate transitions as a result of these interactions. To experimentally realize these conditions, we suggest creating a chain of paramagnetic ions with a J=2 excited state and manipulating it with a five-level optical pumping scheme. Our findings also suggest the possibility of producing a non-Abelian topological state through the interaction of two exceptional points, which would result in the production of bulk-edge correspondence in the system. Ultimately, we outline the requirements for successfully realizing this non-Abelian topological state in the system. Furthermore, we explore the feasibility of using cold atoms to realize the non-Hermitian characteristics of this system, concluding that while this approach can realize some of the necessary conditions, it is unlikely to produce a state with bulk-edge correspondence. Subsequently, we explore the potential roles that $CP$-violation in $CP$-even New Physics states and $CP$-odd charm decays might play in addressing these discrepancies. This study investigates the performance of speech recognition on large-scale 
LibriSpeech datasets, utilizing models pre-trained with different contrastive 
learning approaches. A comparison is made between an earlier method and an 
advanced variant of the method known as Barlow Twins. The results demonstrate 
that contrastive learning can achieve state-of-the-art performance on a range 
of speech recognition benchmarks when combined with a transformer encoder 
architecture. Notably, our findings highlight the potential of applying 
self-supervised learning at an increased resolution, leading to significant 
improvements in downstream task performance. Moreover, our experiments 
indicate that Barlow Twins yields better performance than previous methods 
on multiple LibriSpeech benchmarks, often by margins as large as 2-4 percentage 
points. Ultimately, our best-performing model, trained using 20-second input 
sequences, achieves remarkable performance on a range of speech recognition 
benchmarks, including the out-of-domain test set of LibriSpeech, achieving 
remarkable performance with a word error rate of 2.9%. This represents a 
significant improvement over prior methods, showcasing the potential of 
self-supervised learning for speech applications. A notable advantage of our 
approach is the potential for end-to-end speech recognition at an increased 
resolution, representing a promising area of further research. A codebase and 
pre-trained models are available for public access at the URL https://github.com/ashishgupta21/Barlow-Twin-for-Speech.

Our research focuses on the underlying structure of the Automated Market Makers (AMMs) used in Decentralized Exchanges (DEXs), allowing for an in-depth analysis of the token price formation and transaction fees. We develop a price-based model capturing the essential components of AMM behavior, comprising token liquidity, volatility, and trading activity. This model reveals that the token price relative to the base asset is influenced by the amount of the base asset and volatility, while transaction fees are driven by the volume of transactions and volatility. Notably, our results show that the volatility of token prices has a substantial negative impact on the value of liquidity providers, underscoring the significance of effective risk management for AMMs. Moreover, our analysis highlights the pivotal role of the base asset in AMMs, and we propose an investigation into the characteristics and selection of these base assets. Using empirical data, our approach enables the estimation of volatility and other key variables, and our findings align with those of central bank-driven financial systems, revealing a self-reinforcing mechanism. Ultimately, our model can inform the design of superior Automated Market Makers, aiding both DEX operators and token issuers in making strategic decisions. The integration of Artificial Intelligence techniques and improved data analysis is expected to support the operations of future Internet of Vehicles networks, whose success relies on the management and analysis of massive data from various sources, including vehicle sensors, roadside equipment, and central traffic management systems. Leveraging the potential of these sources, however, poses significant data privacy challenges, particularly in relation to security. To address these concerns, the application of Federated Learning has been proposed to protect IoT data while facilitating the development of accurate machine learning models without exposing sensitive information. This survey aims to provide an overview of the current state and potential applications of FL in IoT networks, with a primary focus on future IoV systems and the associated privacy and security concerns. Furthermore, the study examines the distinct FL approaches within IoV networks, discusses the available security solutions, and identifies key open issues and research directions in this area. Based on these findings, the survey proposes a novel FL framework specifically designed for IoV systems to address the limitations of existing FL techniques and improve the resilience of IoV applications against adversarial attacks. This framework is then validated through simulations conducted in a distributed environment. The results demonstrate that the proposed framework can safeguard IoV applications from attack while ensuring the successful training of local FL models and achieving accuracy rates comparable to that of centralized machine learning, with a notable achievement of over 90% accuracy. This study's findings are expected to contribute to the development of reliable IoV applications using machine learning techniques and address the pressing data privacy and security concerns of future IoV networks. Ultimately, the survey aims to provide valuable insights for researchers and practitioners working in this area. Previous research has highlighted the existence of insecure code in widely-used crypto libraries, but the extent of insecure practices within individual Python projects remains unknown. This study aims to fill this knowledge gap by analyzing real-world Python projects. We conducted a comprehensive review of 500 projects from 8 popular crypto-adjacent repositories on GitHub, examining the usage of 10 crypto APIs and evaluating secure practices in the process. Our key findings include: (1) the majority of projects utilize multiple crypto APIs despite the existence of a single standardized library; (2) a significant majority of projects contain at least one insecure practice; (3) the most prevalent issues are inadequate checks for padding or data errors, and insufficient error handling; (4) approximately 40% of projects demonstrate a need for high security scrutiny due to the presence of severe security missteps. These findings suggest a substantial number of Python projects require heightened security scrutiny. We plan to share our results with the Python community in hopes of fostering improvement. Furthermore, developers can utilize our provided tool to assess the security posture of their own projects. The research is accessible at https://github.com/ferbonte/misusepy. We propose a novel sparse signal deconvolution based seismic reflection inversion method. This technique seeks to extract the subsurface reflection structure from seismic data by reversing the process of wave propagation. Due to the presence of a convolution layer in the forward modeling equation, we employ a deconvolution step to approximate the inverse process. However, conventional deconvolution methods are hindered in the seismic context by missing noise and the necessity to impose constraints on the inverse model due to limited data coverage and extraneous noise. We address these limitations by casting the deconvolution step as a sparse sparse learning problem, where we leverage prior knowledge of the model through group Lasso techniques. This formulation allows us to control the size of the model and impose structural constraints. Understanding universal properties of a critical quantum spin chain model requires analyzing its components, specifically the coefficients of a conformal field theory's operator product expansion. These coefficients are tied to the long-range interactions in the chain and can be determined using the boundary Gaudin model's Bethe state wave functions. By representing the interaction coefficients as distinct terms involving conformal dimensions $\Delta_a$ and $\Delta_b$, and using a integral equation to solve for a function that depends on dimensions and cross-ratio, we gain insight into the general structure of these coefficients. This discovery enables us to derive functional equations for product states in the chain and solve for low-energy spectrum. The obtained results are relevant for the Ising and XX spin chain models. Furthermore, we explore the connection between the coefficients and the central charge of the corresponding conformal field theory. By examining the structure of these coefficients, we can see how they contribute to the analytic properties of conformal field theory at the cross-ratio, thereby shedding light on the phase structure of the critical quantum spin chain models. Automated part-of-speech (POS) annotation is a crucial task for linguistics and natural language processing, typically addressed through machine learning. Although the problem is largely solved for contemporary languages, historical corpora pose significant challenges, primarily due to limited native speaker interaction and a lack of training data. Compounding this issue, historical texts often employ archaic or infrequently used vocabulary that is unfamiliar to even trained models. To overcome these obstacles, we employ a unique combination of innovative techniques and proven methods for the task. Firstly, we utilize cutting-edge neural network architectures pre-trained on large language datasets to generate high-quality POS annotations from existing training data. Next, we integrate these models with state-of-the-art sequence-to-sequence mapping algorithms to generate candidate word forms, replacing unfamiliar words with familiar ones based on contextual similarities. Finally, we utilize trained models to correct automated annotations and the word form replacement algorithm, resulting in substantial improvements across multiple evaluation metrics without the use of manual labels. Notably, our method achieves a notable 89.2% accuracy on a corporate correspondence corpus, rivaling the performance of human annotators. The research demonstrates the effectiveness of combining advanced models with sophisticated algorithms to address long-standing linguistic challenges. This research focuses on developing a method for collecting price response data from non-respondent firms using a market power metric and input price data. We create a testable hypothesis framework for a single candidate demand function based on three key conditions. These conditions being met indicate that a candidate function's total derivative has a positive value, which is necessary for a candidate to be a valid demand function, which can be observed even by a monopolist. We define a scenario in which a firm's price response data, collected through prices and a quantity at a specific point, satisfies a particular inequality if and only if the candidate demand function exhibits a positive total derivative. We apply this approach to a specific type of candidate demand function derived from Generalized Average Partial Derivatives and demonstrate that it includes well-known demand functions such as Stone-Geisser, Brown, and Strecker. Furthermore, we show the results of our method in a simulation experiment demonstrating that our approach accurately detects demand functions that include one or more non-respondent firms with market power. We also present empirical analysis of the demand function for the U.S. beer market using data on prices and beer sales for over 300 products. Applying our approach to this dataset, we found that firms without market power can be identified, which is consistent with our simulation experiment results, whereas firms exhibiting market power were misclassified when their prices were influenced by other factors beyond sales quantity. These findings suggest that firms experiencing external price pressures may still be considered price-takers. Consequently, controlling prices may not always be an effective strategy even though it may not directly influence a company's bottom line. Finally, our analysis also reveals that firms exhibiting market power can maintain a positive profit margin despite not influencing prices. Therefore, controlling prices may not always limit a company's pricing flexibility, which could lead to misinterpretation of market dynamics and an underestimation of the benefits of antitrust actions. In contrast to previous studies, our analysis found that firms exhibiting market power do not always dominate the market, which contradicts the common perception that such companies are typically large. This highlights the importance of considering the market power of non-respondent firms in addition to established leaders. Consequently, companies can develop effective strategies to counter market power by identifying and addressing such situations early on, which can be facilitated by implementing policies before the situation escalates into a full-blown antitrust issue. In conclusion, our research demonstrates the value of collecting input price data in understanding market dynamics and detecting firms with market power, which can be an efficient strategy for antitrust

Our research presents an innovative technique for correcting faults in near-term quantum computing by leveraging the concept of hidden inverses in quantum circuits. By utilizing a specific type of inverse that counteracts a predetermined set of errors, this method offers more efficient error mitigation compared to traditional approaches. We applied this idea to the study of spin systems using the Kitaev model on a honeycomb lattice, focusing on the effects of random Pauli errors. The results indicate that the proposed method is particularly effective for small numbers of errors and indicate the existence of quantum phases without mixing them with classical phases that fade away. This finding is further supported by observing the continuity of the quantum phase diagram even in the presence of errors. Additionally, we found that while the mitigation techniques based on hidden and full inverses yield similar results, the full inverse method exhibits greater resilience to increasing error rates. For larger numbers of errors, the mitigation of full inverses becomes more computationally expensive, making the hidden inverse method a valuable alternative. Overall, this research demonstrates the practical utility of hidden inverses in error mitigation and paves the way for their broader adoption in various applications. As a proof-of-concept, we applied this technique to simulate the quantum annealing process, comparing it to conventional simulations based on time-dependent quantum master equations. The findings confirm that the proposed method accurately captures the essential features of the quantum annealing process, even in the presence of errors. However, the mitigation of full inverses becomes ineffective at high error rates due to the loss of correlation between body and environment, resulting in a failure to accurately describe the system. The current implementation of the proposed method is limited to systems with up to 14 qubits due to computational constraints, and future advancements in computational power will further enhance the applicability of this technique. In conclusion, the presented research provides a valuable tool for correcting faults in near-term quantum computing and contributes to the broader understanding of quantum error mitigation strategies. Future studies will focus on extending the applicability of this technique to larger systems and exploring its potential for simulating complex quantum many-body systems. Furthermore, the method presented here is adaptable to other quantum algorithms beyond spin systems, such as quantum machine learning and quantum cryptography, and could significantly enhance the reliability of these applications. In recent years, deep learning models have been successfully applied to DNA analysis, yet most existing methods treat DNA as a sequence of characters and employ recurrent neural networks, convolutional neural networks, or autoencoders for feature extraction, often in a supervised fashion. These methods are hindered by their fixed, predetermined architectures that fail to account for the innate variability of DNA sequences. Furthermore, the limited capacity of deep neural networks to capture long-sequence information has been well-documented. In response to these challenges, we introduce an unsupervised method for learning a standardized, fixed-dimensional representation of long and variable-length DNA sequences. Utilizing a unique form of denoising autoencoder, our approach leverages DNA's inherent combinatorial properties to project sequences onto a compact, high-dimensional space. Accurately predicting non-performing loans for individual clients is a critical consideration for banks when deciding whether to extend credit. As a result, banks place great importance on assessing the creditworthiness of applicants for personal loans. Past research has shown that factors like income and credit history are crucial indicators of credit risk. However, recent findings from the European Banking Authority indicate a need for banks to give personal loan applications greater consideration. To address this, a model was developed using a dataset of approximately 35,000 applicants from a major Polish bank, incorporating both demographic and credit-related information, as well as additional variables such as loan amount and purpose. The study's results show that these individual characteristics have a significant impact on default risk. Building on this insight, a novel logistic regression model was proposed, known as IP2, which integrates propensity scoring to effectively capture applicants' unique characteristics and prioritize those most relevant to credit risk. The approach involves two stages: initially predicting the propensity score to filter less likely defaults, followed by applying IP2 to retained cases. The comparison with top-performing baseline models revealed that IP2 achieves superior results, yielding an Area Under the Receiver Operating Characteristic Curve of 0.9446 and an 83.25% precision rate. Notably, the model's accuracy gains are largely attributed to a better understanding of corporate clients' behavior, as indicated by loan amount. The proposed model's performance is compared with several alternative credit risk evaluation methods, including decision tree-based models. The findings suggest that while decision trees can effectively capture complex interactions, they fall short of the model's overall accuracy and precision. The research's outcomes are ultimately intended to inform bankers and policymakers on the best approaches to evaluating credit risk and making more informed decisions. Deep Convolutional Neural Networks' (DCNNs) success stems in part from their ability to generate comprehensive image descriptions through learned filters that capture diverse features.  Despite their achievements, DCNNs often struggle with recognizing images in multiple orientations, necessitating the introduction of Deliberate Orientation Networks (DONs) to extract images from multiple orientations for training.  In contrast, Orientation Convolution Networks (OCNs) are regular DCNNs that can learn to recognize images in various orientations without relying on pre-extraction.  By merging DONs and OCNs, Deliberate Orientation Convolution Networks (DOCNs) offer a more efficient solution, achieving better results on existing orientation classification benchmarks while also improving robustness to random orientation perturbations by up to 25%.  Furthermore, DOCNs require fewer parameters and training examples than DONs, demonstrating an enhanced understanding of multi-oriented data through more focused and interpretable filters.  Through analysis of the resulting models, DOCNs are shown to incorporate global orientation awareness and local features, with the global orientation awareness accounting for nearly half of the learned filters.  Additionally, DOCNs generalize well to other low-level image transformations, such as resizing and flipping, making them a valuable addition to existing deep networks.  Finally, DOCNs are successfully applied to multiple tasks, including multi-oriented image classification, multi-instance image classification, and visual question answering, with notable improvements in performance.  As such, DOCNs represent a more efficient and effective approach to recognizing images in various orientations.  Code and model implementations are available at https://github.com/zhpcvision/DOCNNs. Employing the $K$-factor method, we derive the comprehensive $R_{K}$-scale, which encompasses the quark mass $m_q$ and the Jost boundary condition scale $\mu_J$ for flavor $q$. This $R_{K}$-scale integrates out the quark mass hierarchy among the six heavy quark flavors $u, d, s, c, b, t$ to a precision of next-to-leading power. Furthermore, we establish the quark mass distribution among the six heavy flavors up to the next-to-leading power. Additionally, we investigate the pole mass ambiguity, a quantity representing our ignorance of the pole mass relative to the $R_{K}$-scale for a given flavor $q$. This pole mass ambiguity is zero at leading power, resulting in minimal ambiguity. As the power increases, the pole mass ambiguity becomes a periodic function with a periodicity of 6, corresponding to one flavor cycle. The growing concern about post-hatred bias in recommender systems has led to a surge in interest in developing transparent and trustworthy systems that provide understandable explanations to users. Recent research in explainable recommendation (XRec) has primarily concentrated on the quality of recommendations rather than the explanations. In contrast, we focus on the fundamental aspects of user experience in XRec and propose a novel set of explanation guidelines that prioritize user understanding over recommendation precision. We evaluated these explanations with both expert and average users and discovered that explanations conforming to our proposed guidelines received higher user satisfaction ratings. Moreover, our results demonstrate that explanations matching users' expected standards receive higher ratings. Based on these findings, we suggest integrating an explanation quality evaluation metric to balance explanation precision and transparency. We further suggest incorporating this metric into the overall performance assessment of XRec systems. The proposed explanation guidelines can serve as a standard reference for practitioners to improve the transparency and user experience in XRec methods. A thorough examination of electron mobility in an InAs quantum well material is carried out using a combination of experimental and theoretical approaches. The surface morphology of the material is assessed through the analysis of scanning spreading layer microscopy images and correlation with mobility measurements. Additionally, a comprehensive study of electron mobility is performed across a range of temperatures, leveraging a technique called Hall effect measurement. To complement these findings, a precise calculation of electron effective mass is carried out using a highly advanced computational method known as ab initio, and the resulting value is compared to experimental data. The surface roughness of InAs quantum wells is discovered to significantly hinder electron movement. Furthermore, electron mobility is found to follow a distinct temperature trend. Comparisons between the calculated and measured effective masses reveal substantial agreement. These comprehensive findings offer valuable insights into understanding electron mobility in InAs quantum well material. The research results are further discussed in terms of their potential application to enhance the performance of transistors based on InAs surface channels. It is predicted that a reduction in surface roughness combined with an increase in electron energy would lead to improved transistors exhibiting excellent current capacity with minimal noise levels. This predicts a maximum achievable gain in field effect mobility of nearly 100-fold. This theoretical estimate is compared to projected gains in Si-based FETs, which are anticipated to experience a 10-fold increase in field effect mobility. This theoretical analysis provides a valuable framework for the design and optimization of InAs-based transistors. The resulting device is anticipated to possess superior performance capabilities, making it a prime candidate for the development of future high-performance devices. Recent research has focused on developing robust machine learning models that use little to no labeled data. For such efforts, extension of the empirical risk minimization principle, which demands a large amount of labeled data, is required but not feasible always. To bridge this gap, this paper proposes an efficient learning technique that requires only local membership queries (LMQs) from the most vulnerable data points to achieve optimal generalization. The proposed algorithm, based on a novel hybrid method, estimates parameters by combining an upper limit of the robust loss and an upper bound on the loss of remaining data, both calculated using few selected sensitive data points. The proposed technique ensures that its convergence to the optimal generalization error occurs at a polynomial rate with respect to the epsilon value representing data vulnerability. The proposed technique outperformed existing methods in simulated experiments conducted using synthetic data. Furthermore, the practical effectiveness of the proposed technique was demonstrated in real-world applications, specifically, the classification of malicious traffic and the detection of named entity recognition. The proposed technique's performance advantage over existing methods was verified while using the same labeled dataset. Our previous research significantly sped up the time it takes to solve L/U-CoLT systems of equations, going from quadratic to linear time complexity, by introducing a new class of matrices that can do multiplication, addition, and scaling in linear time. In this study, we took that discovery and applied it to finding the inverse of L/U-CoLT matrices, which can now be done in linear time as well. This is particularly useful in our field of computational geophysics, where inverting a matrix is a fundamental operation. To demonstrate its practicality, we showed how to use the inverse of L/U-CoLT matrices to solve nonlinear least-squares problems in linear time, even when the problem is not necessarily convex. Since the problem of solving L/U-CoLT systems of equations is at its core a linear least-squares problem, this research also sheds light on the mathematical properties of L/U-CoLT matrices and their inverse. In addition, we extended the capabilities of the Regnsystemer library to include the inverse of L/U-CoLT matrices and various nonlinear least-squares solvers. As a result, we can now efficiently solve a wide range of nonlinear problems in linear time. To further accelerate computations, we also optimized the time it takes to print complex matrix data, like sparse complex tridiagonal matrices, which are commonly used in numerical methods based on differential equations. By combining linear-time matrix inversion with efficient printing, we significantly reduced the time it takes to print matrices used in finite difference methods. As a result, we can now efficiently solve PDEs like the acoustic wave equation in linear time as well. To showcase this discovery, we created a new version of our acoustic wave solver that runs in linear time and comes with a ready-to-use example. This research was carried out as part of the DANS project 'Efficient algorithms for large-scale geophysical modeling'. In addition to the code for the L/U-CoLT inverse, we also released a new version of our Regnsystemer library that includes the time-efficient printing of sparse complex matrices. Young stars emit powerful X-ray and ultraviolet radiation that interacts with planetary atmospheres, affecting their development and potential habitability. Focusing on M stars, sources of intense stellar flares, our study utilizes the \textit{XMM-Newton} telescope to observe an extraterrestrial flare on the star AD Leo, releasing 10\^10 erg s\^-1. We model this flare in various simulations, combining it with the star's steady ultraviolet and Planck distribution to analyze the impact on planets orbiting M stars at different distances. Our analysis, relevant to terrestrial planets with masses similar to those of Earth, goes up to 10 pc, where planets may exist in a liquid state and experience atmospheric circulation. Our simulations indicate that close planets receive extremely high energy flux, exceeding 10\^4 erg cm\^-2 s\^-1, potentially triggering atmospheric sputtering, altering chemistry, and making it challenging for life to thrive due to surface water loss. Even planets farther away may experience increased atmospheric loss, making water loss a significant factor for planets around active M stars. These processes, particularly atmospheric sputtering, are not typically considered in studies examining the effects of stellar evolution on planetary habitability and water loss, a factor that should be taken into account in such studies. Our research provides a foundation for further exploration into the impact of stellar flares on planetary development and the habitability of planets in the M star exoplanet population. Future applications of this work could involve using the \textit{Astrosat} satellite, \textit{Hinode}, or \textit{RHESSI} to study flares on active stars, refining our understanding and increasing the applicability of our research to a broader population of M stars. Furthermore, observing the impact of high-energy events on planetary development in systems with high-energy events detected directly, such as 55 Cancri e, allows for the validation of our models and the theory of planetary atmospheric loss. Ultimately, the incorporation of these processes into larger models of planetary development and the habitability of planets is necessary to accurately simulate the development and loss of atmospheric water in planets over time. This effect, which can be observed through changes in tunnel current, arises when the quantum dot becomes electronically connected to the island. To study this relationship further, we have developed a method for precisely controlling the quantum dot's electronic state using a nearby gate. However, the island's large size and low critical current mean that the quantum dot's influence on its superconductivity only manifests itself when the tunnel coupling between them is relatively strong. Additionally, we have found that the quantum dot's electronic state can be stabilized by injecting a small amount of normal conductor material into the dot's vicinity. This treatment, which can be controlled using an injection gate, allows for more in-depth exploration of the interactions between the quantum dot and the superconducting island. Furthermore, we have observed that the quantum dot's electronic influence on the island is only partially lost when the tunnel coupling between them is significantly reduced. This behavior suggests that the quantum dot's electronic influence is not solely the result of charge tunneling, but also involves some form of coherent electronic interaction between the quantum dot and the superconducting island. This finding is consistent with previous research that has identified a similar form of electronic interaction as a key component of a recent theoretical model describing the behavior of interacting quantum dots and superconducting islands. Overall, our research provides a more nuanced understanding of the complex electronic interactions between these quantum systems and paves the way for future studies into the emergence of new forms of electronic interaction in these systems at very low electronic temperatures. We explore novel view generation -- the challenge of generating distant, unseen views by virtually navigating a given image -- through a new, efficient technique called DiffDream. It leverages recent advances in image diffusion models, which have made significant strides in generating high-quality images, but have been overlooked in this demanding task. To achieve seamless virtual exploration, we design a model able to generate sequences of sequences, simulating camera movements, by integrating three key components: a condition that adapts to sequential states, an encoder that compresses high-dimensional images, and a decoder capable of attending to these representations. Our results show that DiffDream surpasses state-of-the-art performance in both qualitative and quantitative performance, and we show that it naturally extends existing image analysis models, such as the widely accepted UDA feature tracker. Many complex systems feature networks where interactions between diverse agents combine simple local rules to create complex emergent behaviors. While recent research has found connections between network structure and the underlying dynamic processes, detecting random complex patterns remains a pressing challenge. We propose a new method using topological features to identify stochastic complex dynamics in large networks with multiple local clusters. By analyzing various examples of stochastic complex dynamics, our approach yields accurate and interpretable results. Furthermore, our method is applicable to real-world data analysis, such as an artificial social model and a satellite-tracking experiment. We investigate the temporal Lipschitz stability of solutions to the inverse source problem for the heat equation with a time-varying source. We find that for solutions that lose energy over time due to the source, Lipschitz stability is achieved using measurements within a single time interval. This is in contrast to the situation without energy loss, where stability requires using data from two different time periods. Our study demonstrates that both the growth rate and rate of energy loss due to the source are crucial factors in determining the required time interval for stability. Furthermore, we present numerical experiments to validate our theoretical findings. Crucially, our study shows that the Lipschitz stability constant depends only on the problem and not on the chosen initial or source condition, a highly desirable property in inverse problems. This result is due to the use of a Bessel potential in conjunction with the observability inequality for the adjoint heat equation. This approach has broader applications, as illustrated by our derivation of Lipschitz stability for the inverse source problem for the Schr\"odinger equation under specific conditions on the domain's geometry and the source function. A notable extension of our work involves using the Bessel potential in conjunction with the finite difference of potential differences of two solutions to obtain Lipschitz stability for the more challenging case of a space-dependent source, although this approach requires additional constraints on the source function. For the case of a space-dependent source, we also derive the necessary conditions for its existence in terms of the domain's geometry and the source function's properties. These conditions have significant implications for the construction of a stable and consistent variational method. Our study provides a novel approach to the inverse source problem for the heat equation by formulating it as a two-variable optimization problem. This approach leverages the existing theory of Lipschitz optimization and allows for the construction of a stable and consistent optimization algorithm. Our results are illustrated with numerical experiments that validate our theoretical findings and demonstrate the stable convergence of the optimization algorithm to the solution of the problem. This approach has broader applications and can be used for other inverse problems, as illustrated by our derivation of Lipschitz stability for the inverse problem of recovering the time-dependent velocity field from the steady-state Navier-Stokes equation under specific conditions on the boundary conditions and the domain's geometry. Multi-input multi-output (MIMO) networks attempt to improve ensemble performance by training separate sub-networks within a unified base model and combining their predictions.  Despite this, the resulting ensemble has a high parameter redundancy, which can hinder efficiency and scalability.  In this work, we investigate whether we can decrease the parameter redundancy of MIMO ensembles through a more coordinated approach, where a single MIMO network is split into distinct components that share most of their parameters.  Through theoretical analysis, we established a lower bound on the required parameter redundancy to achieve a specified level of error probability.  This is done by ensembling basic networks with a high failure rate, and using a MIMO network designed to minimize the probability of failure.  Our findings also indicate that the existing MIMO approach suffers from a poor use of parameters.  To validate our theory, we modified the MIMO approach to reduce the parameter redundancy by introducing shared components.  This is done by having each layer process data through different gates, allowing the network to share most of the weights.  Our experiments on the CIFAR10 dataset demonstrate the effectiveness of our method, leading to parameter reductions of up to 85% while maintaining similar test accuracy levels.  For instance, the modified approach using ResNet32 blocks requires 0.73 million parameters, which is 85.7% fewer parameters than the baseline MIMO approach also using  ResNet32 blocks.  This reformulated MIMO approach also outperforms the state-of-the-art in terms of scalability, achieving a speedup of 3.3 times when trained on a V100 GPU with the same number of parameters.  To further verify our theory, we also applied our method to larger datasets, such as ImageNet, and observed similar results.  Our code is available at https://github.com/asharakeh/Shared-MIMO. We're contributing to this research by: 1) developing a statistical framework to analyze how past health conditions influence future health states; 2) using Bayesian inference to update this model as more data becomes available. In contrast to other approaches, our framework allows us to analyze the effects of past health on both specific and general health states, making it more adaptable. We also demonstrate that our model can be extended to analyze various health states and previous exposures, not just general past health. We test the framework using simulated data and real-world data from the UK's Born In Bradford study, focusing on how early life exposure to smoking affects respiratory and cardiovascular diseases later in life. Our results show that our approach provides accurate estimates and is more adaptable than other models. We also compare the performance of our framework with other statistical methods using simulated data. We found that our approach consistently produced the best results and was more robust than other methods. Additionally, we found that incorporating data on specific early life exposures, not just overall exposure, is crucial in understanding their long-term effects. We cannot confirm the association between early life smoking and respiratory diseases, but we found a significant link to cardiovascular diseases. We propose a new method that helps the model learn to cope with such noisy labels by simultaneously estimating the clean labels and improving the model, leveraging an additional clean validation set for accurate guidance. Experimental results on multiple medical image datasets confirm the effectiveness of this approach, which outperforms existing methods in handling noisy labels across various levels of error present in the datasets. Our method is particularly effective when the majority of the labels in a dataset are accurate, accurately estimating the clean labels in the process. Furthermore, this approach is versatile and can be applied to a wide range of learning tasks, including those with mixed label noise or more complex multi-channel datasets. In a total functions logic such as HOL, certain non-terminating functions are difficult to define directly. To overcome this limitation, a clock mechanism is often introduced to enforce termination after a specified evaluation depth. While commonly regarded as cumbersome, we argue that alternative methods of adding a clock exist, with varying levels of intrusion. We present a new approach that simplifies termination proofs without unduly utilizing the clock mechanism, particularly illustrated through the context of functional big-step semantics for programming language interpretations. This method involves defining termination properties within separate axiomatic theories for each evaluation step and importing only the necessary results into the main context. As a result, the burden of the clock mechanism is minimized, and termination proofs become more straightforward. We demonstrate this technique by applying it to the evaluation step of small-step semantics in an imperative language example. Further, we extend this method further to consider clock representation and the big-step semantics example for an imperative language. Furthermore, we apply the same strategy to the evaluation step of small-step semantics in a functional language and the big-step semantics example for a functional language. The findings show that this method outperforms traditional methods in HOL. Furthermore, we propose a new approach called axiom-based clock, which simplifies termination proofs for functions that loop forever. To compare the clock representation approach with the axiom-based clock approach, we apply both methods to the evaluation step of small-step semantics in an imperative language and the big-step semantics example for an imperative language. The findings show that the axiom-based clock approach outperforms the clock representation approach. Ultimately, we argue that the choice of method depends on specific termination proof requirements. While the axiom-based clock approach is more suitable for simple termination proofs, the clock representation approach is more suitable for complex termination proofs. Furthermore, we argue that the clock representation approach is more general than the axiom-based clock approach. Furthermore, we propose a new approach called clock reasoning, which simplifies termination proofs for functions that loop forever. The Sgr A East supernova remnant, located near the center of the Milky Way, poses a mystery with age estimates ranging widely from 10,000 to 10 million years; its precise timing remains uncertain. Observations of the 2.0-2.1 GHz HII regions within the remnant, obtained through the Five Hundred Parsec Array, reveal a primary emission mechanism of radio recombination lines and continuum radiation. Analysis of the Raman-scattered light suggests that the gas is ionized by a compact, energy-rich source, potentially a stellar or an intermediate-mass black hole, that is not currently visible due to extinction. Estimating the ages of the surrounding HII regions, based on the rates of gas loss and ionization, places their lifespan between 10,000 to 30,000 years. This self-consistent age range aligns with the existing spectrum of nearby X-ray emissions originating from the core of Sgr A East, making it plausible that the remnant is a relatively young system, born in the past 10,000 to 30,000 years. Given the relatively low luminosity of the primary energy source, it is unlikely that it would be observable even at the high sensitivity of the Five Hundred Parsec Array. The study examines various oversampling methods to classify multi-class topics, particularly focusing on the performance of SMOTE, a popular method for generating new samples based on minority class examples, and its two variants along with random oversampling in text classification tasks. The research assesses the efficiency of SMOTE, its Borderline and ADASYN modifications, and random oversampling in conjunction with machine learning algorithms such as k-nearest neighbor, support vector machine, and different types of neural networks, using text representations. The outcomes suggest that using oversampling methods enhances the accuracy of classification and indicates that the performance of k-nearest neighbor is significantly improved with the use of ADASYN, whereas the accuracy of support vector machine is boosted with the use of SMOTE's borderline variant. For neural networks, the results show that the accuracy of randomly sampled data with SVM is higher than that of ADASYN, a machine learning algorithm known for its performance with class imbalance problems. The study further reveals that the proposed approaches exhibit consistent results across different datasets used in the study. The research concludes that the choice of oversampling method and the pairing of algorithms is crucial for enhancing the performance of classification tasks. The study suggests that the use of SMOTE, a simple and efficient method, paired with SVM, a robust algorithm, yields the best outcomes among the examined combinations. The research provides insights into the performance of different oversampling methods and machine learning algorithms, sheds light on the current state of research in this field, and contributes knowledge to experts in this area. The outcomes of the study can be utilized by practitioners to choose the most suitable method for their specific problem and select the best pairing of methods for optimal results. The research further offers suggestions for future investigations in this area. The study's findings are made available to the research community through its execution of experiments and provision of results, facilitating the replication of the study and its outcomes. The study's results have been published in a proceedings paper and presented at the 12th International Conference on Text Recognition and Understanding (2019). This study investigates the relationship between COVID-19 news coverage and the pandemic's spread across the United States by leveraging a detailed dataset of daily local and national news articles and death rates from 2020-2021. Our analysis reveals that local news coverage initially outpaced the national death rates but eventually converged. Conversely, national news coverage initially trailed the national death rates but subsequently closed the gap. Furthermore, we found that local news coverage was more responsive to specific regions' death rates, whereas national news coverage was more influenced by overall national trends. By examining the content of local and national news articles, we determined that they primarily focused on non-local aspects, underscoring the significance of regional news coverage in conveying pandemic-relevant information. Our findings also highlight the differential impact of the pandemic on local communities, implying that effective communication and information strategies are needed to mitigate the spread of the virus, especially in under-resourced regions. Ultimately, our research emphasizes the critical role that local news outlets play in informing the public about the evolving pandemic situation. We develop a novel, efficient learning method, which integrates both reinforcement and imitation learning techniques. It leverages synthetic data generated based on prior knowledge embedded within the environment. This synthetic data serves as the training base for imitation learning. To mitigate systematic measurement errors on noisy quantum simulators, researchers employ measurement error mitigation (MEM) techniques. However, the performance of these methods is highly dependent on the specific noise model present. For the purpose of training against real-world errors, the popular anti-finishing scheme has been developed. This work presents an alternative to existing schemes, the multi-kick scheme, which outperforms anti-finishing in the sense that it can accurately mitigate errors associated with any number of noisy gates, regardless of gate pairing. This new method leverages the use of Fourier transforms, which allows for the effective cancellation of errors resulting from long sequences of gates. The multi-kick scheme has been successfully tested on a range of quantum circuits, including those designed by Microsoft Quantum, OpenQASM, and QuLA. The results demonstrate the effectiveness of this method in providing a more accurate noise model, which in turn enables the efficient classical simulation of noisy quantum circuits. This new approach has significant potential for applications requiring the simulation of deep quantum circuits, particularly in the context of quantum algorithms and roadmapping. For mobile robots to successfully navigate unfamiliar surroundings independently, having an effective mapping system is crucial. Current mapping approaches rely heavily on state estimation techniques that minimize drifting and provide accurate representation of environmental features, but are challenging in situations where reliable GPS data or stable platforms are not available. This research proposes an innovative mapping method inspired by the principles of localisation and mapping in biological systems, specifically the global positioning and wayfinding abilities of ants. This ant-inspired method, called swarm mapping, has been implemented and tested alongside traditional SLAM techniques in similar robotic platforms on various navigation tasks, resulting in the emergence of promising patterns that suggest reduced drifting and improved robustness when using the proposed swarm approach. Furthermore, when the largest available sensor range possible is used, the results indicate that the proposed swarm method exhibits robustness in the absence of, or under severely impaired, sensor functionality. Ultimately, the findings suggest that the proposed swarm approach has significant potential for enhancing mobile robot navigation performance in complex and unpredictable environments. The proposed swarm method is based on a simplified ant navigation model and uses a place recognition sensor-matching loss to build and refine the map. To facilitate the evaluation of the proposed swarm approach, the research also introduces an open-source framework enabling the parallel simulation of various robotic localization and mapping algorithms on a cluster of computing nodes. This framework, specifically tailored for the evaluation of probabilistic localization and mapping methods, allows for the parallel generation of diverse random seeds in real-time to simulate different robotic scenarios, and currently supports the evaluation of up to 100 distinct seed scenarios per minute on a 100-GPU cluster, or 6-8 seeds per second using a single GPU, thereby greatly reducing the evaluation time required for various probabilistic localization and mapping methods. The research demonstrates the effectiveness of the proposed framework in facilitating the parallel evaluation of algorithms using real data from robotic sensors, and showcases its potential to accelerate the evaluation of methods based on vision, inertial, and LiDAR sensor data by up to 2 orders of magnitude, thereby significantly reducing the time required for algorithm development and testing. The proposed framework is intended to support the evaluation of a wide range of localization and mapping algorithms, and is currently available for download at the provided URL. We investigate how electron spillover and nonlocal behavior affect light propagation between two adjacent metallic areas and compare this to a quantum hydrodynamics model. We demonstrate that a quantum hydrodynamics model that accounts for electron spillover but assumes local behavior fails to produce a consistent solution within the e-hydrodynamics framework, leading to field divergence in certain cases. However, incorporating nonlocal behavior resolves this issue, enabling us to analyze wave propagation between two metallic areas with controlled electron spillover characteristics. This is then applied to a realistic model of a graphene-hBN-molybdenum disulfide heterostructure, where nonlocal nonlocal quantum hydrodynamics accurately models the interaction between these materials. Ultimately, this research lays the groundwork for developing an accurate nonlocal quantum hydrodynamics model of realistic spillover profiles. Furthermore, it suggests that even small nonlocality can greatly improve the accuracy of simulations, particularly for microscopic scales where nonlocal effects may become more pronounced. Additionally, it is found that quantum hydrodynamics models are unable to accurately capture the interaction between the p-type semiconductor molybdenum disulfide and the n-type semiconductor h-BN, but this issue is resolved when a nonlocal model is used. The results also indicate that quantum hydrodynamics models may fail to accurately predict the interaction between the p-type semiconductor molybdenum disulfide and the n-type semiconductor multi-layered stack when electron spillover is considered, but this limitation is removed when nonlocal behavior is accounted for. However, it is found that even nonlocal hydrodynamics models may fail to accurately capture certain features of light interaction with two-dimensional materials at specific wavelengths due to the simplified nature of these models. Despite some limitations, the research demonstrates the potential of nonlocal hydrodynamics models to accurately capture the complex interaction of light with two-dimensional materials and suggests that such models may be useful in the development of future photonic devices based on these materials. Ultimately, the results indicate that hydrodynamics models can be a useful tool for simulating and designing new 2D material-based photonic devices. Furthermore, the results show that nonlocal hydrodynamics models are particularly well-suited to analyzing and designing devices that utilize the unique properties of transition metal dichalcogenides, which are known to have unique optical properties. Electrolyte is a crucial component of numerous biological systems, which rely heavily on electrical interactions.  In an attempt to better grasp the behavior of ions in these systems, this research focuses on understanding the electrical properties of thin electrolyte layers adjacent to charged surfaces.  A key factor influencing these properties is the solvation of the solvent, which affects the electrostatic potential.  To investigate this, the authors employed a classical, atomistically modeled system consisting of a monovalent salt in a solvent surrounded by a charged wall.  By simulating a system in equilibrium, the authors observed a thin, solvent-dominated layer near the wall, which exhibited a high concentration of oppositely charged ions.  The authors then used Poisson-Boltzmann theory to calculate the electrostatic potential and compared it to the results obtained from explicit solvent simulations.  Although the models showed some discrepancies, the explicit solvent simulations revealed a clear, periodic pattern in the electrostatic potential, which was in agreement with the predictions made by a mean-field approach.  These findings suggest that mean-field approaches can be an effective, computationally efficient way to understand the behavior of thin electrolyte layers.  However, the models used in this research did not account for ion size or non-electrostatic interactions.  As such, the findings may not be directly applicable to systems that rely heavily on non-electrostatic interactions, such as biological systems.  Future research aims to investigate the role of non-electrostatic interactions in these systems.  A key benefit of the mean-field approach is its ability to greatly reduce computational costs, which could be particularly valuable in the study of large, biological systems.  As such, the findings presented here could have important implications for our understanding of biological systems. Our approach is versatile and can be adapted to other datasets with similar characteristics and sizes. By streamlining this process, we can significantly reduce the time and resources required to identify requirements, enabling more efficient software development. Next, the outcomes are applied to evaluate the energy efficiency in a general, single-hop network with multiple relays and network coding, considering both the best and average outcomes among all possible coding vectors. The analysis shows that, although MDNC offers benefits in terms of outage probability and capacity, it may not always enhance energy efficiency in comparison to a scenario with no network coding, where the energy efficiency is determined solely by the best outcome among all possible coding vectors. Ultimately, our findings reveal that the influence of the magnetic impurity on the surrounding superconductivity is more nuanced than initially thought. Techniques for registering point clouds from different scenes have had notable success, but many current methods are designed for static scenes and can struggle with dynamic objects that move significantly between frames.  To mitigate this issue, researchers have developed methods that use motion information, but these approaches often rely on pre-existing maps to determine where to apply the registration and can't deal with complex scenes that appear multiple times.  In this research, we present a new framework called CED-Registration that can register point clouds from different scenes without prior knowledge, by using object-centric scene graphs to describe pre- and post-scene object positions.  Our approach can register any two point cloud samples from any scene graph description, and we've successfully tested it on a new benchmark consisting of scenes from the NuScenes dataset with object movements of up to 20 meters.  Our results show that our approach, currently limited to two-dimensional graph descriptions, outperforms current methods across the entire dataset.  Additionally, we've developed a new metric for evaluating registration performance in scenes with moving objects and used it to compare the effectiveness of different local optimization methods.  Our code and the new benchmark are available at https://github.com/asharakeh/ced-registration. Overfitting is another major issue, particularly when working with smaller datasets. Across all evaluation benchmarks, the method surpasses previous techniques, with improvements ranging from 2% to 9% for specific metrics. Notably, the method outperforms current best results in the literature by 5% for specific metrics, with a substantial gain of 9% for the Volume metric. A novel type of metric comparison analogous to Alexandrov comparison is established, 
and its relationship to optimal transport between measures on a Riemannian manifold 
is demonstrated. Specifically, defining the MTW condition (where MTW stands for 
M\"{u}ller-Melrose-Warren) and a notion called weakly MTW-cyclic, it's shown that 
the MTW comparison is preserved when taking limits in a pointed Cheeger-Gromov-Horing 
convergence sense for Riemannian manifolds. Furthermore, for measures on a 
manifold, being MTW-cyclic in relation to their total boundary of optimal maps 
implies convergence under weakly Cheeger-Gromov convergence along with convergence of 
various boundary and transport costs. Warren and M\"{u}ller initially introduced 
the MTW condition as a refinement of the Ricci curvature lower bound. However, 
this note presents a novel formulation of MTW that is comparable to Alexandrov 
curvature bounds without reliance on previous results and shows that it results in 
the same class of manifolds. Moreover, combining MTW with a notion called strict MTW 
leads to a new notion of strict MTW-cyclic which, along with further assumptions, 
yields a stronger form of convergence called strict Cheeger-Gromov convergence. 
Interestingly, MTW is proven to be a local property and can be deduced from a 
neighbourhood metric inequality. Also, MTW is shown to be a generalisation of 
Ricci lower bounds as demonstrated by its application to the standard 2-sphere. 
Lastly, a local structure theorem for the MTW condition has been presented. It 
describes a condition for a neighbourhood of a point on a Riemannian manifold to be 
MTW-cyclic when the measures are confined to that neighbourhood and its boundary. 
This local structure is characterised by the manifolds being uniformly locally 
Euclidean. Moreover, it has been shown that if an MTW-cyclic region contains measures with 
support entirely within its interior, then those measures result in uniform 
convergence. As a direct application of this characterisation, it has been shown that 
MTW is preserved under the process of blowing up along a submanifold. In a broader 
context, it has been shown that MTW is preserved when transferring measures from one 
manifold to another via a pullback operation, provided the total boundary of

This led us to investigate the efficacy of soft quantization in reducing parameter updates by converting floating-point model weights to integer values, thereby enabling bulk parallelizable integer training with reduced floating-point parameter updates obtained through sampling integer weights around the original floating-point values. Building on this idea, we developed an algorithm that combines top-performing initial integer weights, along with an innovative method for determining optimal integer representations of floating-point weights, which significantly enhances the model's performance when compared to traditional methods like fine-tuning or batch-wise quantization. Notably, our proposed approach yields superior results even when trained under a data augmentation constraint, successfully applying parameter-efficient tuning to pre-trained models such as ResNet50 and ViT-L/14 across various downstream tasks. This research marks the first parameter-efficient tuning application to vision tasks, offering a promising avenue for updating large-scale pre-trained models with substantial cost reductions. Source code is available at https://github.com/ale XS/PE-T. Ultimately, we were able to update the pre-trained ImageNet weights of the top-1 model by ~1GB (0.53% improvement) with only 4.8% of the floating-point parameters over 5 epochs on the ImageNet dataset with a 32 GPU cluster, achieving a remarkable outcome. Transformer-based language models have been shown to struggle with logical reasoning, especially when it involves negation. Unlike previous studies, this research finds a positive outcome: it demonstrates that these models can easily process negation when it's explicitly marked in the input. We call this phenomenon "negation sensitivity." Our analysis reveals that this sensitivity is caused by the models' tendency to associate negation with grammatical patterns, rather than semantic meaning. Specifically, we found that the models rely heavily on the part of speech of negation and its position in the sentence to determine how to process it. Furthermore, we note that the models' ability to handle negation in a limited sense may not necessarily indicate true understanding of negation. We propose a new approach to assessing the models' ability to comprehend complex language concepts. Our findings have significant implications for how we evaluate and develop transformer-based language models in the future. Ultimately, we argue that the models' performance in processing negation is not a straightforward indication of their semantic intelligence. We suggest that their capabilities in processing other complex concepts, such as causality, should be reevaluated as well. Our study serves as a cautionary tale for how previous misinterpretations of the models' abilities can lead to an exaggerated understanding of their true semantic capacity. We conclude that the models' ability to comprehend human language is still a topic of debate and requires a more nuanced assessment than currently provided. In neural machine translation, the attention mechanism is the most widely applied technique, enabling models to identify relevant source sentence parts when translating a target word. However, existing evidence suggests that these models often rely more on their own past translations rather than the source sentence when generating target words. This poor performance is due to the separation of encoding and generating processes in traditional NMT models, causing delays in attention mechanisms and inconsistent distributions over source words. To address this issue, a new approach called DELTA Transformer is proposed, which integrates an encoding layer into the traditional Transformer decoder. By merging these components, delays are eliminated, and a new attention mechanism called DELTA is introduced. This DELTA attention, unlike its predecessor, consistently uses all available source words when generating every target word, eliminating dependencies on past target words. Experiments conducted on four language pairs demonstrate significant performance enhancements, with gains of up to 2.1 BLEU points, and improvements over state-of-the-art results in two of the language pairs, outperforming the Universal Transformer with deltablue scores of 35.1 for English to German and 42.1 for Bulgarian to English. Furthermore, this work reveals the existence of a sweet spot for DELTA attention span, and future research directions are identified, including the application of the proposed DELTA attention mechanism to low-resource NMT. The DELTA Transformer code is publicly available at the GitHub repository https://github.com/ashishnileshgupta/DELTA-Transformer. Figures and additional analysis can be found at https://ashishnileshgupta.github.io/DELTA-Transformer. The experiments were performed using the Universal Transformer code released by Jiasun Feng, which can be accessed at https://github.com/jiasunfeng/universal-transformer. All experimental results were obtained on a machine with 40 CPU cores and does not include results from GPU trials. The time complexity of the proposed model is directly related to the number of target tokens, with a value of O(n^2) in the case of correct DELTA attention spans and O(n) when using large DELTA attention spans. The experiments were performed in collaboration with the MIT NLP group led by Philip Metzger and the Rutgers NLP group led by Ashish Nitin. The data for the Bulgarian dataset was kindly provided by the Bulgarian State Agency for Language Policy. Cosmologists have proposed an inflationary model where the universe's exponential growth can be theoretically explained. It's essential to understand how this model relates to the physical world, particularly how it can be tested with observations. Researchers have suggested that oscillations in the inflaton field might serve as a signature of this model, even if these oscillations remain hidden from us. It's assumed that three things occur: (1) the inflaton field quickly settles into its minimum state after inflation; (2) the kinetic energy of the inflaton field is negligible compared to its potential energy; and (3) the inflaton field behaves classically. It's been argued that oscillations aren't a reliable signature of this model, as they likely become trapped in a state of quantum zero-point vibrations rather than settling into their minimum state. However, this conclusion may be incorrect. By re-examining the concept of equilibrium in statistical mechanics, particularly with respect to the concept of observables, it's been shown that oscillations don't necessarily settle into their minimum state but instead continue indefinitely. Nevertheless, the oscillations' effects on the universe are likely too small to be detected. It's possible that while oscillations might not serve as a reliable signature of this model, they still offer valuable insights into the more general case where the universe's signatures can be either oscillatory or static. In fact, many inflationary models fall into this category, and oscillations might still be detectable in these models. It's also been shown that while the oscillations' effects on the universe's density perturbations are unlikely to be detectable, the oscillations' impact on the universe's curvature radius might be more significant in certain models, potentially offering a new way to test inflationary models. These findings highlight the importance of understanding the differences between equilibrium in statistical mechanics and relaxation processes, as well as the need to be more precise in defining what we consider "observable" in cosmology. They also underscore the more general applicability of the arguments presented here, potentially offering new avenues for exploring and understanding the universe's origins. In the long run, a more in-depth exploration of these topics might still hold the key to directly observing the remnants of oscillations, a phenomenon that could revolutionize our understanding of the universe. The arguments presented here primarily focus on the classical oscillations of a single inflaton field but suggest that similar issues might arise in more complex field theories, particularly those with multiple fields, potentially offering new ways to test inflationary models and observe their signatures more directly

This paper aims to provide a clear overview of recent developments in solving equilibrium problems via fixed-point methods, as well as some fixed-point algorithms designed for single-valued mapping solutions. It also offers a starting point for exploration into the broader categories of generalized fixed-point problems and their associated iterative methods. Fixed-point algorithms for equilibrium problems were initially introduced by Yao and Chen in 2007, serving as a foundational study in this field. This overview will delve into the advancements that have taken place over the past decade, covering issues like existence and algorithms for solving equilibrium problems, as well as their variants. It will also discuss recent developments in generalized fixed-point methods, offering new insights and suggestions for future research in this area. Furthermore, it highlights some notable contributions from scholars like Blumennfelder, Chandra, Nadeau, Noutsos, and Smaros in this field. 
In conclusion, this paper will offer practical advice and highlight potential areas for further research within the context of fixed-point algorithms for equilibrium problems.
